messages.text: You don't hope you're forgiven. You have it, according to the riches of His grace.
messages.explanation:
"In Him we have redemption through His blood, the forgiveness of sins, according to the riches of His grace." "Have" is present and active in Greek, and the word also means to hold fast and possess. Hold on to it, because people will try to talk you out of it.

The first-century church was marked by bold, certain faith: "through this Man is preached to you the forgiveness of sins." Some today call that certainty presumption and doubt humility. But God didn't forgive cheaply; redemption was paid with Jesus' blood. Lay out all of God's riches and you still won't reach the end of how forgiven you are.

messages.text: The servant forgiven millions grabbed a man who owed him a few thousand. He never really heard that he'd been forgiven.
messages.explanation:
Facing ruin, the servant begged, "Be patient with me, and I will pay you all." He couldn't have repaid it in a lifetime, but he still believed he could. The king had compassion and cancelled the entire debt. Yet straight away the man went out and seized a fellow servant by the throat over a small sum.

He walked away still thinking in terms of paying, not in terms of being forgiven. Some believers are forgiven but never enjoy it, so they have nothing to give others. When you really take in how much you've been released from, you'll want to release everyone around you.

messages.text: Before the cross: forgive, so you'll be forgiven. After the cross: forgive, because you have been.
messages.explanation:
Jesus told His Jewish hearers, before His death, "If you do not forgive men their trespasses, neither will your Father forgive your trespasses." After the cross, Paul writes to believers: "forgiving one another, even as God in Christ forgave you": a completed, once-for-all act.

Threatening people with "forgive or you won't be forgiven" gives them no power to do it. The only firm foundation for forgiving others is knowing how completely you've been forgiven. Bitterness loosens its grip when you're overwhelmed by grace.

messages.text: Seventy times seven doesn't mean 490. It means stop counting.
messages.explanation:
Peter thought he was being generous: "Lord, how often shall my brother sin against me, and I forgive him? Up to seven times?" Jesus answered, "Not seven times, but seventy times seven." Seven is the number of perfection, so this is perfection multiplied: without limit.

Any marriage, family or friendship will need this. There will always be something new to forgive. Couples who say "we'll never need to forgive each other" haven't been married long. Draw from the forgiveness you've received, and keep no record.

messages.text: Prayer is simply holding out an open hand.
messages.explanation:
God gave mankind free will, and He doesn't override it, not even to bless us. He's ready with favour, wisdom and health, but He waits for our consent. Prayer is that consent: an open heart, an open mind, an open hand. We bring nothing; He brings everything.

That's why even "Amen" is a prayer: "so be it." Jesus said keep on asking, keep on seeking, keep on knocking. Not to wear God down, but to keep your hands open to a Giver who loves to give.

messages.text: "Your Father knows what you need before you ask." Jesus' conclusion wasn't "so don't bother" but "therefore, pray."
messages.explanation:
Some people reason that if God already knows everything, there's no point praying. But Jesus drew the opposite conclusion: "Your Father knows the things you have need of before you ask Him. In this manner, therefore, pray."

We live in a fallen world with a real enemy, and God has chosen to work through His people's asking. When answers are slow, it isn't God holding back; there may be a battle. Keep asking, not desperately, as if God needed persuading, but confidently, because you know Him.

messages.text: Jesus' prayer at Lazarus' tomb took a few seconds. Power isn't in the length of the prayer, but in the One you pray to.
messages.explanation:
"Father, I thank You that You have heard Me. And I know that You always hear Me." Then: "Lazarus, come forth!" Jesus never criticised a short prayer, but He did rebuke the Pharisees for long, showy ones, and warned against "vain repetitions" by those who "think that they will be heard for their many words."

You don't need to pray louder, longer or harder to twist God's arm. He gave His Son before anyone asked. Talk to Him simply, like a child to a father: "Father, I need Your help with my son. Heal him, in Jesus' name."

messages.text: Daniel read that the seventy years were up, and then he prayed. God's promises invite you to take part.
messages.explanation:
Jeremiah had prophesied that Judah's captivity would last seventy years. Reading it in the very year the seventy were complete, Daniel didn't sit back and say "whatever will be, will be." He set his face toward the Lord in prayer and supplication.

God loves participation. Even blessings that seem to come automatically usually have a story behind them: a grandmother, a friend, someone praying in the Spirit who didn't even know whom they were praying for. When you pray, you're no longer earthbound; you can touch situations on the other side of the world.

messages.text: God gives to all liberally and without reproach: always giving, never finding fault.
messages.explanation:
"If any of you lacks wisdom, let him ask of God, who gives to all liberally and without reproach." In Greek, both "gives" and "without reproach" are continuous. God is constantly giving, and constantly not finding fault with you. He's like the sun, which pours out far more warmth than the earth can ever absorb.

Is that the God you grew up with? Your faults were laid on Jesus at the cross, and His worthiness is credited to you. So ask for wisdom in earnest, not as a cliché. Wisdom isn't age or experience; Pharaoh had the dream, but Joseph had the interpretation.

messages.text: God gave His Son unasked, while we were His enemies. How will He not give lesser gifts to His friends who ask?
messages.explanation:
"He who did not spare His own Son, but delivered Him up for us all, how shall He not with Him also freely give us all things?" The Holy Spirit argues from the greater to the lesser. Healing, provision and protection are all smaller gifts than Jesus; why would God hold them back?

He gave the greatest gift without being asked; will He refuse lesser gifts when you ask? It cost Him dearly; the rest cost Him nothing. He gave it when we were enemies; we are now His friends. And "shall" points to the present and the future: He will keep showing Himself as the great Giver.

messages.text: Jabez's whole prayer was "bless me… enlarge my territory… keep me from evil," and God called him more honourable than his brothers.
messages.explanation:
Some say it's selfish to pray for your own blessing, prosperity or protection. Yet in two short verses, a man whose name meant "pain" asked God to bless him, enlarge his territory, keep His hand on him and keep him from evil. "And God granted him what he requested."

Read aloud, the prayer takes about fifteen seconds. God calls Jabez "more honourable" (the Hebrew kavod: weighty, glorious). People who won't ask God to provide often scheme to provide for themselves. Ask in simple, earnest faith.

messages.text: God told David, "If that had been too little, I would have given you much more." You have not because you ask not.
messages.explanation:
After David took Bathsheba and arranged her husband's death, God reminded him through Nathan of all He had given: the kingdom, the throne, everything. "And if that had been too little, I also would have given you much more!" David grabbed what he could have asked for.

James says we covet, fight and quarrel because we don't ask. If something in your life feels like it's lacking, even your marriage, don't grasp or nag. Talk to the God who would gladly give you more.

messages.text: The Lord restored Job's losses when he prayed for his friends.
messages.explanation:
Job's three friends had wounded him with accusations, and God was displeased with them. So He told them to bring an offering to Job and let Job pray for them. "And the Lord restored Job's losses when he prayed for his friends. Indeed the Lord gave Job twice as much as he had before."

The turnaround came as Job turned his attention outward, and toward people who had hurt him. If you're waiting for your own breakthrough, pray for someone else's. Release the people who misjudged you. Restoration often comes through that door.

messages.text: Don't judge God by the middle of Job's story. Look at the end: the Lord is very compassionate and merciful.
messages.explanation:
"You have heard of the perseverance of Job and seen the end intended by the Lord: that the Lord is very compassionate and merciful." Job's 42 chapters can feel long, but most of it is conversation. His trial itself lasted months, not decades.

At the end, God blessed Job's latter days more than his beginning: twice the livestock, ten more children, and daughters more beautiful than any in the land. He lived another 140 years and saw four generations. Whatever chapter you're in, the end God intends for you is good.

messages.text: Job's friends argued from experience, tradition and rules. Their words were partly true, but wrongly applied, and they only made things worse.
messages.explanation:
Eliphaz argued from experience: "Who ever perished being innocent?… Even as I have seen." Bildad argued from tradition: "Inquire of the former age… consider the things discovered by their fathers." Zophar argued from legal logic: "If you would prepare your heart… if iniquity were in your hand, put it far away."

Their principles sounded right, but truth applied to the wrong person at the wrong time does harm. Their speeches only hardened Job. By chapter 29 he refers to himself over forty times and to God only a few. If you want to help a hurting friend, don't come with your experience, tradition or rules. Bring them God.

messages.text: Job longed for a mediator who could lay one hand on God and one on him. You have one: Jesus.
messages.explanation:
"Nor is there any mediator between us, who may lay his hand on us both," Job cried. In his day, there was no one to stand between a suffering man and a holy God and plead his case.

Today there is: "one Mediator between God and men, the Man Christ Jesus." One of our own sits at the Father's right hand, a glorified Man whose heart still beats with human sympathy because He suffered as we do. Whatever you're going through, you have an Advocate in heaven.

messages.text: "Deliver him from going down to the pit; I have found a ransom." Then: "His flesh shall be fresher than a child's."
messages.explanation:
Elihu, the young man who spoke last, describes a person wasting away, bones sticking out, near the gates of death. Then: if a messenger, "one among a thousand," comes "to show man God's uprightness," not the man's own record, God is gracious and says, "Deliver him… I have found a ransom."

The result: "His flesh shall be young like a child's; he shall return to the days of his youth." God can be righteous in healing and restoring sinful people because He found a ransom: His own Son. Don't point a suffering person to their failures. Point them to the ransom.

messages.text: Every time Satan moved against God's people, he ended up running into God, and serving God's purpose.
messages.explanation:
He tempted Adam and Eve, and God announced the Seed who would crush his head. He sought to sift Peter like wheat, and Peter came out strengthened to strengthen his brothers. He accused and attacked Job, and Job ended up meeting God and being doubly blessed.

Above all, he thought the cross was his triumph over the Son of God, and the cross became the instrument that saved us all. The enemy thinks he's dealing with a weak saint, and keeps meeting a mighty God instead.

messages.text: You don't have to wait until chapter 42. Say it now: "Lord, You are right. Everything I have is from You."
messages.explanation:
Job's trouble exposed a root of self-righteousness in a genuinely good man: "I was eyes to the blind and feet to the lame." When God finally spoke, He didn't list Job's faults; He showed His own majesty in creation. And Job said, "I have heard of You by the hearing of the ear, but now my eye sees You."

God disciplines His children with His word and sometimes with disappointing circumstances, but not with disease or disaster. Why take the long road? Agree with Him now. Drop the need to be right, in your marriage too, and you'll find a peace that self-justification never gives.

messages.text: An inheritance isn't earned. It's handed down because you're family.
messages.explanation:
"In Him also we have obtained an inheritance." An inheritance doesn't come by effort, performance or achievement. It comes because someone loves you and counts you as family. It depends entirely on the giver.

And it isn't only for eternity. One worship leader, stuck in a holiday car-park queue, glanced at this verse and simply said, "Lord, I have an inheritance." Moments later a car pulled out right beside him. God's blessings are meant to touch the daily grind of life, here and now.

messages.text: "He who is bathed needs only to wash his feet." You're saved once; the Word washes off the dust of the day.
messages.explanation:
Jesus used two different Greek words: being bathed all over, and having your feet washed. The bath is new birth, cleansing by His blood, once and for all; you can't be born again and again. "You are completely clean," He said.

But walking through the world, your feet pick up dust: what you hear at the salon, see on a screen, absorb at work. That's what His word is for. "You are already clean because of the word I have spoken to you." Don't go days without it. Even a few minutes in the Word refreshes you like cool water on tired feet.

messages.text: Jesus cleanses His bride by speaking to her as already glorious, without spot or wrinkle. Husbands, speak to your wives that way.
messages.explanation:
Christ "gave Himself for her, that He might sanctify and cleanse her with the washing of water by the word, that He might present her to Himself a glorious church, not having spot or wrinkle." "Present" is continuous in Greek: He keeps presenting her as already glorious, never making her feel dirty or old.

The world bombards your wife with messages about how she should look and who she should be. A husband washes those away with his words: "You're beautiful to me." It isn't flattery; it's how God sees her in Christ. And He loved first, before asking anything in return.

messages.text: You fell in love by speaking kind words to each other. Do the first works again, and you can fall in love again.
messages.explanation:
Jesus told a church that had left its first love: "Repent and do the first works." Not "feel the first feelings," but do what you did at the beginning. The principle applies to marriage. Couples fall out of love the same way they fell in: by their words, only now they're critical instead of kind.

Start saying please and thank you again. Send a message that says you miss her. Listen without judging. Be the one who charms your own spouse, before someone else tries to. Act in faith, and the feelings will follow.

messages.text: His friends had fled and denied Him. Jesus' first words to them after the resurrection were "Peace be with you."
messages.explanation:
The disciples were hiding behind locked doors, afraid. Three of them had slept while He agonised in Gethsemane. All of them had scattered when the soldiers came, and Peter had sworn he never knew Him. This was their first meeting with the risen Lord.

He stood among them and said, "Peace be with you." Not a word of reproach. That's how He speaks to you after you fail. And it's how you can carry yourself: when you feel the anger rising, don't release it. Words spoken in anger are almost never the ones you'd choose.

messages.text: Righteousness is "unto all and upon all who believe." Jesus died for everyone; it rests on those who receive it.
messages.explanation:
Some teach that Jesus died only for a pre-selected few. But Paul says the righteousness of God through faith in Jesus Christ is "unto all and upon all them that believe." It is offered to all, because Christ died for all, and it comes upon those who believe.

In the parable of the hidden treasure, the man didn't just buy the treasure; he bought the whole field, and Jesus said elsewhere that the field is the world. The gospel isn't a closed door. Whoever believes receives.

messages.text: The law demands that you become what you're not. Grace invites you to live out what you already are.
messages.explanation:
God doesn't say, "Act like a king and you'll become one." He says you already are a king and a priest in Christ: now walk it out. He doesn't say, "Behave and you'll be forgiven." He says you are forgiven: now live forgiven.

It's far easier to live out what you already are than to strain to become what you're not. That's the difference between law and grace. Every time you open the Bible, let Jesus remind you who you already are in Him.

messages.text: You're a child of light. You may do something dark, but you never become darkness.
messages.explanation:
"You are all sons of light and sons of the day. We are not of the night nor of darkness." Some teaching leaves believers feeling that they slip in and out of the light many times a day. But a prince can do a pauper's work and still be a prince; a man can act like a monkey and he's still a man.

Sin is never good for you, but it doesn't change what you are. If you've been born again, you are a son or daughter of the day, and that's a settled identity, not a daily verdict.

messages.text: When thick darkness covered Egypt for three days, "all the children of Israel had light in their dwellings."
messages.explanation:
The darkness was so thick that the Egyptians couldn't see one another or move from their places. Notice: if Israel's light had come from lamps or candles, the Egyptians could have lit theirs too. It was a supernatural light, a gift of grace, given only to God's people.

Isaiah 60 says that in the last days darkness will cover the earth, but the Lord will arise over you. Whatever darkness covers the world, your nation or your street, God's people can have light in their homes and families.

messages.text: Walking in the light is where you are, not how well you're doing. That's why the blood is still cleansing you there.
messages.explanation:
"If we walk in the light as He is in the light, we have fellowship with one another, and the blood of Jesus Christ His Son cleanses us from all sin." It doesn't say "according to the light," as though it were measured by your obedience. No one could walk according to the light God has. It's about location.

And if walking in the light meant not sinning, why would the blood need to keep cleansing us there? When a believer has a bad thought or says a wrong word, they don't drop into darkness and have to climb back. They're in the light, and the blood keeps them clean.

messages.text: Jesus said His followers "shall not walk in darkness," a double negative in Greek: certainly never.
messages.explanation:
"I am the light of the world. He who follows Me shall not walk in darkness, but have the light of life." The Greek "ou me" is the strongest possible negative: no way, never. It's used sparingly, in places like "I will never leave you" and "blessed is the man to whom the Lord shall not impute sin."

The same John later writes about someone who hates his brother and walks in darkness. He's describing someone who claims to be in the light but isn't; as he says, "they went out from us, but they were not of us." For the one who truly follows Jesus, darkness is not your address.

messages.text: God said "Let there be light" on day one. The sun wasn't made until day four.
messages.explanation:
The first time Scripture records God speaking, He says, "Let there be light." But the sun, moon and stars came on the fourth day. So what was that first light? In Hebrew, "let there be" (yehi) begins with yod and hey, the first two letters of God's covenant name, a hint that the light is from Himself.

Jesus is the light of the world, the light that was there before the sun. Things often look darker at night; worries and sickness feel heavier after sunset. But you're not a child of the night. Your light doesn't depend on circumstances; it's a Person.

messages.text: The Holy Spirit is God's down payment, His guarantee that He's coming back for all of you, body included.
messages.explanation:
You were "sealed with the Holy Spirit of promise, who is the guarantee of our inheritance." The Greek word means a deposit: in the ancient marketplace, if you bought something too big to carry, you paid a deposit as a pledge that you'd return to collect it.

The one blessing no believer can have yet is the new body: immortal, never tired, never sick, never ageing, like Jesus' risen body that could be touched and could eat fish. Until then we trust God for health and strength. And the Spirit inside you is His promise that the full redemption is coming.

messages.text: The Jews sought light, the Greeks sought knowledge, the Romans sought glory. All three shine in the face of Jesus Christ.
messages.explanation:
"God who commanded light to shine out of darkness has shone in our hearts to give the light of the knowledge of the glory of God in the face of Jesus Christ." In Paul's day the Jews looked for light and revelation, the Greeks pursued wisdom and philosophy, and the Romans chased military and imperial glory.

People today still chase the same three: mystical enlightenment, education and knowledge, and fame or wealth. Paul says every one of them is found in one place: the face of Jesus. Put Him at the centre of your life, your marriage and your parenting, and you'll find what everyone else is looking for.

messages.text: The cure for a lonely heart is to be alone with Jesus.
messages.explanation:
There's no misery like a lonely heart, and loneliness isn't about whether someone is beside you. You can be married and still be lonely; it's an empty heart. The Samaritan woman came to the well at noon to avoid people, and God arranged that even the disciples were away buying food. She was alone with Jesus.

Loneliness and aloneness aren't the same. Time alone with the One who knows everything about you and still draws near fills the empty place. Talk to Him about your day: when you're angry, tempted, sad. He loves to spend that time with you.

messages.text: Nicodemus came to Jesus by night; Jesus went to the Samaritan woman at noon. He humbled the theologian and lifted up the sinner.
messages.explanation:
Put John 3 and John 4 side by side. A respected male teacher of Israel versus a Samaritan woman with five former husbands. He came secretly at night; Jesus met her in broad daylight. He sought Jesus; Jesus sought her. He opened with "Rabbi, we know…" and was told, "You must be born again… Are you the teacher of Israel and do not know these things?"

But to her, Jesus wrapped the truth in compliments: "You have well said… in that you spoke truly." Every valley will be lifted up and every mountain brought low. Grace flows like water to the lowest places, so stay humble.

messages.text: Most Jews took the long way around Samaria. Jesus "needed" to go through it, because one lonely woman was there.
messages.explanation:
Travelling from Judea to Galilee, religious Jews would cross the Jordan and walk around Samaria rather than through it. But John says Jesus "needed to go through Samaria." The only need was a woman who had been looking for love in all the wrong places.

Notice what had just happened: the religious leaders in Judea had rejected Him. God's love doesn't turn bitter when it's refused; it simply goes looking for someone who'll receive it. If you think you're too far gone for Him to come your way, remember Samaria.

messages.text: Jesus never told Nicodemus He was the Messiah. He told a Samaritan woman, "I who speak to you am He," literally, "I am."
messages.explanation:
When the woman said, "I know that Messiah is coming… He will tell us all things," Jesus answered, "I who speak to you am He." In the Greek, "He" isn't there: "I am," the very name God gave Moses at the burning bush.

The great teaching on true worship, worship in spirit and in truth, wasn't given to a religious leader but to a woman with a broken history. She dropped her water pot, ran back to the town she'd been avoiding, and became an evangelist on the spot: "Come, see a Man who told me all things that I ever did."

messages.text: Jacob prophesied that Joseph would be "a fruitful bough by a well, whose branches run over the wall." Jesus sat at Jacob's well, by Joseph's land, and blessed a Gentile.
messages.explanation:
John notes that Sychar was "near the plot of ground that Jacob gave to his son Joseph," and that Jacob's well was there. Centuries earlier, Jacob had blessed Joseph: a fruitful bough by a well, its branches reaching over the wall. The wall pictures the separation between Jew and Gentile.

Jesus, the greater Joseph, sat by that well and His blessing reached over the wall to a Samaritan. And He did it while weary and resting. If He blesses like that when He's tired, imagine what He does now, strong and seated at the Father's right hand.

messages.text: Numbers 21 hides John 3 and John 4 together: the bronze serpent lifted up, then a well where Israel sang, "Spring up, O well!"
messages.explanation:
Jesus told Nicodemus, "As Moses lifted up the serpent in the wilderness, even so must the Son of Man be lifted up." That's in Numbers 21. And in the same chapter, Israel turned toward the sunrise and came to Beer, which means well, where God said, "Gather the people, and I will give them water," and they sang to the well.

The serpent story happens, as it were, at night, like Nicodemus coming in the dark. The well comes after they face the sunrise, like the woman at noon. God hid both pictures of Jesus side by side, long before John wrote them down.

messages.text: When your debt is paid, you can open the ledger and laugh. People who know they're forgiven don't need to be defensive.
messages.explanation:
A businessman deep in debt can't bear to look at his accounts; it's all red. Then a wealthy friend pays everything off and leaves a surplus. Now he opens the ledger and laughs: "I owed that much? Look at that!" Every line fills him with gratitude toward his benefactor.

We get defensive ("You're the same!") when we're not sure we're forgiven. When you know the debt is paid, you can admit a fault freely: "It's not you, it's me. Pray for me." That's why the woman at the well could tell the whole town about her past.

messages.text: It's never the Lamb that's too small. It's always our appetite.
messages.explanation:
At the first Passover, God said that if a household was too small for a whole lamb, they should share it with their neighbours. The household might be too small, but never the lamb. God's supply always exceeds the demand: after five thousand were fed, there were still twelve baskets left over.

In Jesus' parable of the great supper, after the poor, the lame and the blind were brought in, the servant reported, "It is done as you commanded, and still there is room." Jesus is worth more than all mankind put together. His sacrifice is big enough for you, with plenty to spare.

messages.text: God's invitation isn't "Come and help prepare." It's "Come, for all things are now ready."
messages.explanation:
"A certain man gave a great supper and invited many, and sent his servant at supper time to say, 'Come, for all things are now ready.'" The Son prepared this feast with His own blood, and on the table is everything you need: healing, deliverance, wisdom, favour. Jesus even called healing "the children's bread."

Free doesn't mean cheap; it means priceless. Yet the invited guests made excuses: one had bought land he hadn't seen, another oxen he hadn't tried. Don't be too busy to come to a table that Heaven itself has set for you.

messages.text: If your ox fell into a pit, you'd pull it out first. Jesus saw sick people the same way: no interrogation, just rescue.
messages.explanation:
At a leading Pharisee's house on the Sabbath, where everyone was watching Him closely, Jesus healed a man with dropsy. Then He asked, "Which of you, having a donkey or an ox that has fallen into a pit, will not immediately pull him out on the Sabbath day?" They had no answer.

We sometimes come to the edge of someone's pit with questions: "Have you confessed all your sins? Have you forgiven your mother-in-law?" Jesus didn't. He saw people who had fallen and needed pulling out. "Freely you have received, freely give."

messages.text: Luke 14 has three parables of demand: count the cost. Luke 15 has three parables of grace: the sheep, the coin and the son, all found.
messages.explanation:
In Luke 14, Jesus is in a Pharisee's house, surrounded by people jockeying for the best seats and crowds following Him as a teacher to copy. To them He says: hate your family, carry your cross, count the cost of the tower, weigh your army before the war. If you want Him as a pattern to imitate, those are the terms.

Then Luke 15 begins, "Then all the tax collectors and sinners drew near to Him." The moment people came to Him as Saviour, His heart opened up into the most beautiful parables He ever told. Discipleship matters, but it's never above sonship. The word "disciple" doesn't appear in the New Testament after Acts.

messages.text: Scripture doesn't say the angels rejoice. It says there's joy in the presence of the angels: the joy of the God who found you.
messages.explanation:
All three parables in Luke 15 end with joy, and in every one it's the finder's joy. The shepherd lays the sheep on his shoulders rejoicing and calls his friends: "Rejoice with me!" The woman finds her coin and throws a celebration. The father runs to his son.

The parables don't dwell on how the lost were feeling. They tell us how God feels. Heaven is made happier by sinners coming home. And how did the sheep "repent"? It let itself be found and carried. That's the heart of repentance: consenting to be loved.

messages.text: No one in heaven will be there merely as an invited guest. Every one of us was compelled to come in.
messages.explanation:
After the first guests refused, the master said, "Go out into the highways and hedges, and compel them to come in, that my house may be filled." God doesn't override our will, but He makes us willing. One morning Zacchaeus felt like climbing a tree to see Jesus; that was grace drawing him.

It's tempting to think we weighed up the options and wisely chose Jesus. But Jesus said, "No one can come to Me unless the Father who sent Me draws him." If you can see what others can't, it's because He opened your eyes. That leaves no room for pride, only gratitude.

messages.text: "Be imitators of God as beloved children." Children who know they're loved copy their father naturally.
messages.explanation:
The word for imitators is "mimetes," the root of mimic. And the word for dear children is "agapetos," beloved: the same word the Father used of Jesus at His baptism. Paul isn't saying "copy God so you'll be loved"; he's saying beloved children copy their father.

That makes parenting simple: make sure your children know they're loved, then watch your own life, because they'll copy you, even your bad habits. And it makes Christian living simple: start each day receiving His love and His saving, and imitation follows.

messages.text: Jesus didn't say, "Sin no more, and then I won't condemn you." He said, "Neither do I condemn you; go and sin no more."
messages.explanation:
When her accusers had all slipped away, Jesus asked the woman caught in adultery, "Where are those accusers of yours? Has no one condemned you?" "No one, Lord." The only person present without sin, the one who could have thrown the first stone, said, "Neither do I condemn you; go and sin no more."

He didn't excuse her sin; He paid for it, because one day it would be laid on Him at the cross. The church often gets the order backwards. It's the gift of no condemnation that gives you the power to go and sin no more.

messages.text: John 8 opens with a sinner set "in the midst." It ends with Jesus passing "through the midst." Grace takes the centre.
messages.explanation:
The scribes and Pharisees brought the woman and "set her in the midst," a sinner on display, the centre of attention, to trap Jesus. The chapter ends with them picking up stones to throw at Him, and Jesus "going through the midst of them," passing by unseen.

It begins and ends with stones, and it begins with sin in the centre and ends with the Saviour in the centre. Religious minds keep sin at the centre. When Jesus is at the centre of your life, your marriage and your thinking, sin loses its place on the stage.

messages.text: When challenged about the law, Jesus wrote on the ground with His finger: the same finger that wrote the law on stone.
messages.explanation:
The religious leaders thought they had Him cornered. If He said "Stone her," where was His message of grace? If He said "Don't," He was breaking Moses' law. Jesus stooped down and wrote on the ground with His finger, just as the tablets at Sinai were "written with the finger of God." He was the Lawgiver.

Then He stood and said, "He who is without sin among you, let him throw a stone at her first," and stooped to write again. One by one, from the oldest to the youngest, they left. The law's light, turned on her accusers, exposed them all.

messages.text: The first sword in the Bible blocked the way back to Eden. The last one fell on the Shepherd, and the way home is open.
messages.explanation:
After the fall, God placed cherubim and "a flaming sword which turned every way" to guard the way to the tree of life. Justice barred sinful man from God's presence, for his own sake.

The last mention of a sword in the Old Testament is "Awake, O sword, against My Shepherd… Strike the Shepherd." Jesus, carrying all our sins, walked into that sword. Judgment found its resting place in His body. Now the voice says, "Come home," and the way in is called "new and living": the nearer you come, the more you live.

messages.text: You can't sweep darkness out of a room. You let the light in.
messages.explanation:
As a boy, one preacher rolled over a boulder by the sea and found a nest of tiny scorpions underneath. He ran off, scared. When he came back, the sun had been shining on that spot, and they were all gone.

Some habits, fears and depressions won't go however hard you fight them. Let the light shine in. David said, "I have more understanding than all my teachers, for Your testimonies are my meditation." They had more knowledge; he had more light. The more of Jesus you see, the less room darkness has.

messages.text: A baby's tears in a basket moved Pharaoh's daughter, and set a nation's deliverance in motion.
messages.explanation:
Pharaoh had ordered every Hebrew baby boy to die. Moses' mother put him in a basket among the reeds, trusting God. Pharaoh's own daughter came down to bathe, opened the basket, "and behold, the baby wept. So she had compassion on him."

Nothing is smaller than a baby's tears, yet God used them to save the boy who would deliver Israel. Years later, God asked Moses, "What is that in your hand?" It was just a shepherd's staff, and it became the rod of God. Never think you're too small for God to use.

messages.text: Jesus did His first miracle not in Jerusalem at a feast, but in tiny Cana, to save an unnamed couple from embarrassment.
messages.explanation:
If Jesus had had a publicist, the first miracle would have been staged in Jerusalem during a great feast, near the temple, before thousands. Instead it was at a village wedding in Cana, still a small town today, where the wine had run out. The bride and groom aren't even named.

He didn't do things for show; He did them to meet needs. The God of eternity laid in a manger, grew up in lowly Nazareth, and turned water into wine for a peasant couple. Can we stoop to serve our own families the same way, and sometimes just bite our lips instead of insisting on being right?

messages.text: Running from God, Jonah went down to Joppa, down into the ship, down into the sea. Away from God is always down.
messages.explanation:
God told Jonah to go east to Nineveh; he headed west for Tarshish instead. Scripture traces every step: he "went down to Joppa," "went down into the ship," "went down into the lowest parts of the ship," was thrown down into the sea, and was swallowed into the belly of a great fish.

Even then, God used him: the frightened sailors ended up worshipping the Lord. And Jesus Himself pointed to Jonah's three days in the fish as a picture of His own burial and resurrection. If you've been heading down, turn around. With God, the direction is always up.

messages.text: "Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they do." Jesus placed His executioners under the offering for sins of ignorance.
messages.explanation:
The law made a provision for someone who sinned unintentionally, in ignorance: they could bring an offering. On the cross, Jesus found the one thing His enemies had going for them, that they didn't truly know what they were doing, and pleaded it before the Father.

It was after hearing this prayer that one of the thieves, who had been mocking Him, changed and said, "Lord, remember me." That's the heart of the One who died for you: even while being crucified, He was looking for grounds to forgive.

messages.text: When the soldiers came for "Jesus of Nazareth," He answered "I am," and they fell to the ground. No one took His life; He laid it down.
messages.explanation:
A detachment of armed soldiers and temple officers came to Gethsemane with lanterns and weapons to arrest one man. When Jesus answered, "I am He" (literally "I am," the name God gave Moses at the burning bush), "they drew back and fell to the ground."

The captive waited for His captors to get up. Jesus said, "No one takes My life from Me, but I lay it down of Myself." The cross wasn't an accident or a martyr's tragedy; it was God's plan, freely embraced by a Son who loved you.

messages.text: Stephen saw Jesus standing at God's right hand, not seated, as if ready to return if Israel would only receive Him.
messages.explanation:
Elsewhere the risen Christ is described as "sat down at the right hand of the Majesty on high." But as Stephen preached to the leaders of Israel, his face shining like an angel's, he looked up and said, "I see the heavens opened and the Son of Man standing at the right hand of God."

The offer of the kingdom was still open. Instead they covered their ears and stoned him, and Stephen died praying, "Lord, do not charge them with this sin." At the foot of that execution stood a young Pharisee named Saul, whom grace would soon turn into its greatest apostle.

messages.text: Acts 8, 9 and 10 record three conversions: an Ethiopian, a Jew and a Roman. Noah's three sons, Ham, Shem and Japheth, all reached by grace.
messages.explanation:
All the nations descend from Noah's three sons: Ham (associated with Africa and the Near East), Shem (the Semitic peoples, including Israel) and Japheth (associated with the peoples who spread to Europe). Right after Stephen's death, Luke tells three conversion stories in a row.

In chapter 8, an Ethiopian official (from Ham's line) is baptised. In chapter 9, Saul of Tarsus (from Shem) meets Jesus. In chapter 10, Cornelius, a Roman centurion (from Japheth), receives the Spirit. The mystery of the church had begun: one new people in Christ, from every family of the earth.

messages.text: Sometimes God says, "Don't keep telling Me about the mountain. Speak to the mountain."
messages.explanation:
God "put all things under His feet, and gave Him to be head over all things to the church." Jesus is far above every name that is named, including the name of any diagnosis. And He has given His people His name, like a power of attorney: it's not how much you have, but how much the One you represent has.

Pray to God with thanksgiving and ask Him for wisdom. But when it comes to sickness that Jesus has already borne, speak to it in His name, the way a traffic officer raises a hand to stop a truck. The authority isn't in the officer's size, but in who stands behind him.

messages.text: One of Jesus' names, "El Gibbor," means Mighty God: God the Hero.
messages.explanation:
"His name will be called Wonderful, Counsellor, Mighty God, Everlasting Father, Prince of Peace." In Hebrew, Mighty God is "El Gibbor": El is God, gibbor is a mighty warrior, a champion, a hero. The angel Gabriel's name comes from the same root.

The world dreams up superheroes with special powers who save one city or one person. Yours is real. He gave His life to rescue the whole world, and He's never let anyone down. Your children need to know this Hero above every star and celebrity.

messages.text: "Noah found grace." His name means rest. Rest finds grace in the eyes of the Lord.
messages.explanation:
This is the first time the word grace appears in the Bible, and it's attached to a man whose name, Noach, means rest. In a world filled with violence and corruption, one man found favour with God.

Grace isn't only for people who have fallen deep into sin; Jesus never sinned and He was full of grace. Grace flows to those who rest in God rather than striving. If you want more of His favour, don't try harder; rest more fully in what He's done.

messages.text: "Cover it inside and outside with pitch." The Hebrew words come from the same root as atonement.
messages.explanation:
God told Noah to cover (kaphar) the ark inside and out with pitch (kopher). The usual Hebrew word for pitch or tar is different; this word comes from the same root used for atonement, the covering of sin. The ark wasn't just waterproofed; it was "atoned" inside and out.

The ark is a picture of Jesus. When the fierce waters of judgment fell on the whole earth, not one wave touched those inside. On the cross, Jesus could say, "All Your waves and billows have gone over Me." They went over Him so they would never go over you.

messages.text: Noah didn't shut the door of the ark. "The Lord shut him in."
messages.explanation:
When every creature had gone in, two by two, Scripture says "the Lord shut him in." Notice the name: it's Yahweh, the covenant name, not just Elohim the Creator. As far as the world was concerned, He was God; to Noah, He was the Lord who keeps covenant.

When God closes the door, no one can open it: not a preacher, not a demon, not your own failures. If the journey gets rough and you stumble, you fall inside the ark, not out of it. Put your children in His hands too, and trust Him to keep them.

messages.text: Look around and you'll be distressed. Look within and you'll be depressed. Look to Jesus and you'll be at rest.
messages.explanation:
God designed the ark's window at the top, not around the sides. Noah's family wasn't meant to stare out at the destruction around them, but to look up. In the wilderness, Israel simply followed the cloud by day and the fire by night, and God watched over everything else.

The enemy either gets you to look around at the bad news, or to look inside at your own thoughts and failings. Don't let him. Look up to the glorified Man at the Father's right hand, who understands you and represents you.

messages.text: God said "Come into the ark," and later "Go out of the ark." He went in first and came out last.
messages.explanation:
If someone says "Come in," where are they? Inside. When the flood began, God didn't say "Go into the ark"; He said, "Come into the ark, you and all your household." He was already there. When it was over, He said, "Go out of the ark." He was still inside, the last to leave.

That's the mark of a true hero: first in and last out. Whatever storm you're heading into, God doesn't send you in alone. He's already there waiting for you, and He won't leave until every one of His own is safely out.

messages.text: The Hebrew word for rainbow is the archer's bow. After the flood, God hung up His bow in the sky.
messages.explanation:
"I set My bow in the cloud." The word is the same one used for a warrior's bow. God was saying, in effect, "I've put down My weapon." And a rainbow only appears when storm and sunshine meet: when trouble comes and God's grace shines on you, look for it.

Isaiah 54 takes it further, right after the suffering Servant of Isaiah 53: "As I have sworn that the waters of Noah would no longer cover the earth, so have I sworn that I would not be angry with you." Every rainbow is a reminder of a promise sealed at the cross.

messages.text: Noah was safe because the ark was safe. It's not how good you are; it's how good your Ark is.
messages.explanation:
After more than a year, everyone who went into the ark came out alive: Noah, his wife, his three sons and their wives, and every creature, "according to their families." Not one was lost, not even to natural death. The safety of those inside depended entirely on the ark.

Your safety depends on Christ, not on how well you held on. Live to honour Him, yes, but as the fruit of being saved, not the root. Your life "is hidden with Christ in God," and He has never lost anyone placed in His care.

messages.text: When they lifted up their eyes, they saw no one but Jesus only.
messages.explanation:
On the mountain, Moses (the lawgiver) and Elijah (the restorer of the law) appeared in glory beside Jesus. Peter, wanting to honour them all, offered to build three shelters. The Father interrupted him from a bright cloud: "This is My beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased. Hear Him!" Him, not them.

The disciples fell on their faces, terrified. When they looked up, Moses and Elijah were gone. Their time had served its purpose; the day of the Son had come. Let that be the focus of your life: no one but Jesus only.

messages.text: "Arise, and do not be afraid." In Greek, "arise" is passive: let yourself be lifted up.
messages.explanation:
Right after the Father said, "Hear Him," the disciples lay trembling on the ground. You might expect Jesus' first words to be a stern command. Instead, "Jesus came and touched them and said, 'Arise, and do not be afraid.'" The verb is passive: not "get yourself up," but "be raised."

He didn't only speak; He touched them and lifted them to their feet. That's the voice of grace. Whatever has knocked you down, the One the Father says to listen to is saying to you, "Let Me lift you. Don't be afraid."

messages.text: When the bride described her Beloved, others asked, "Where has He gone, that we may seek Him with you?"
messages.explanation:
The daughters of Jerusalem asked the Shulamite, "What is your beloved more than another beloved?" She answered with a portrait: "My beloved is white and ruddy, chief among ten thousand… his eyes are like doves… he is altogether lovely." And the questioners became seekers: "Where has your beloved gone, that we may seek him with you?"

There's a place for urging people to love the lost and serve God. But the deepest motivation comes from within, from seeing how lovely Jesus is. Talk about Him the way she did, and people who are hungry will want Him too.

messages.text: "Then the sons are free," said Jesus about the temple tax. Then He paid it anyway, with a coin from a fish's mouth, "for Me and you."
messages.explanation:
When the tax collectors asked whether Jesus paid the temple tax, Peter said "Yes" too quickly, treating Jesus like any ordinary worshipper. Jesus gently pointed out that kings don't tax their own sons; the temple was His Father's house. "Then the sons are free" (sons, plural, because we share His sonship).

Then, so as not to offend, He sent Peter to catch the first fish that came up, and in its mouth was a coin, the exact amount for two. The Creator summoned the wealth of the lake, and humbly paid for Peter too. Majesty and meekness, together in one Person.

messages.text: Moses ended in failure; Elijah ended in discouragement. Of the Messiah it was written: "He will not fail nor be discouraged."
messages.explanation:
Moses, the great lawgiver, lost his temper at the end and struck the rock, and couldn't enter the promised land. Elijah, the great prophet, ended up under a tree after fleeing from Jezebel, telling God, "I alone am left." Even the greatest men have feet of clay.

Isaiah prophesied of God's Servant: "A bruised reed He will not break… He will not fail nor be discouraged." Jesus was patient with Peter's blunders and wasn't crushed by Samaria's rejection; He went all the way to the cross. Put the greatest heroes beside Him, and they all fade.

messages.text: On the mountain, Moses and Elijah spoke with Jesus about His death, which Luke calls the "exodus" He would accomplish.
messages.explanation:
Of all the topics they could have discussed in that blaze of glory, Moses and Elijah talked about "His decease which He was about to accomplish at Jerusalem." The Greek word is "exodus," His departure. And notice the verb: not a death that would overtake Him, but one He would accomplish.

The greatest subject in heaven is the Lamb who was slain. Moses led one exodus out of Egypt; Jesus' exodus through the cross and resurrection leads all who believe out of sin, condemnation and death.

messages.text: Before the three shelters of glory there had to be three crosses on another hill. He came down the mountain for you.
messages.explanation:
Peter said, "It is good for us to be here," and would have stayed in the glory for ever. But Jesus came down Mount Hermon and set His face toward Golgotha. Before He would be flanked by Moses and Elijah in glory, He'd be flanked by two thieves in shame. The face that shone like the sun would be spat on; the garments that blazed white would be gambled for.

He could have gone back to heaven alone from that mountaintop. Instead He chose to go down, so He could bring you with Him.

messages.text: In Nazareth, Jesus stopped reading mid-sentence, at "the acceptable year of the Lord." You live inside that comma.
messages.explanation:
Isaiah 61 says the Messiah would come "to proclaim the acceptable year of the Lord, and the day of vengeance of our God." When Jesus read it aloud in the synagogue, He stopped right after "the acceptable year of the Lord," closed the book and sat down.

Between that comma and "the day of vengeance" lie two thousand years of grace. This is the season of God's favour, when the good news goes out to every nation. Jesus knew exactly where to stop, and so should we: today is not a day of wrath for you, but the year of His welcome.

messages.text: You're not waiting for the Antichrist. You're waiting for Jesus.
messages.explanation:
The grace of God teaches us to live "looking for the blessed hope and glorious appearing of our great God and Saviour Jesus Christ." The blessed hope isn't a terrifying figure or a time of catastrophe; it's a Person.

"Having now been justified by His blood, we shall be saved from wrath through Him." The cross already absorbed God's wrath against your sins. So when you read the news and the world grows darker, lift your head. Your Saviour is coming for you.

messages.text: "I will come again and receive you to Myself, that where I am, there you may be also."
messages.explanation:
Jesus spoke these words in the upper room, hours before His arrest. He was the one about to be betrayed and crucified, yet He was comforting the disciples who would soon run away: "Let not your heart be troubled."

In a Jewish betrothal, the bridegroom went away to prepare a home for his bride, then came back to fetch her, at a day and hour she didn't know. Jesus has gone to prepare a place for you in His Father's house. He isn't coming to deal with your sins; He dealt with them once for all. He's coming for His bride.

messages.text: "The Lord Himself will descend." Not an angel, not a messenger: Himself.
messages.explanation:
Paul could have written simply "the Lord will descend." Instead, the Holy Spirit chose "the Lord Himself." It's a word of warmth that runs through Scripture: "He Himself took our infirmities." On the Emmaus road, "Jesus Himself drew near." "The Son of God, who loved me and gave Himself for me."

The best part of His coming isn't streets of gold or the end of sickness, wonderful as those are. It's this: "and thus we shall always be with the Lord." Heaven wouldn't be heaven without Him, and He's coming in person for you.

messages.text: "In a moment" translates the Greek atomos: an instant so small it can't be divided.
messages.explanation:
"We shall not all sleep, but we shall all be changed, in a moment, in the twinkling of an eye, at the last trumpet." The word for moment is atomos, the root of our word atom, meaning indivisible. The change will be instantaneous.

This corruptible body will put on incorruption, and this mortal body will put on immortality: no more aging, sickness or fatigue, and no more stumbling into the things you're ashamed of. Your body is the one part of your salvation still to come, and Jesus has already paid for it.

messages.text: The last time the disciples saw Jesus, His hands were raised, blessing them. He'll return the same way.
messages.explanation:
"He lifted up His hands and blessed them. Now it came to pass, while He blessed them, that He was parted from them and carried up into heaven." The angels then said, "This same Jesus, who was taken up from you into heaven, will so come in like manner."

He didn't leave scowling or with a warning finger raised. He left with His hands stretched out over His people, and He hasn't lowered them since. That's how He wants you to picture Him today: blessing you, loving you, always.

messages.text: It's not the sheep's job to take care of the shepherd. "The Lord is my shepherd; I shall not lack."
messages.explanation:
Sheep aren't known for their brains, but they are loved, fed and protected, as long as they stay with the shepherd. There's no such thing as a wild sheep; a sheep was never meant to look after itself.

God knows the cares on your shoulders and your daily responsibilities. Come under His care and let Him be your Shepherd. When the Lord is your shepherd, the next words follow as surely as night follows day: you shall not lack.

messages.text: You're never taller than when you look up.
messages.explanation:
With five loaves, two small fish and thousands of hungry people in front of Him, Jesus "looked up to heaven, and blessed." That's the posture God made us for. The enemy wants you looking around: comparing, competing, envying. When Peter asked about John, Jesus said, "What is that to you? You follow Me."

Looking up is true humility. It says, "I can't, but He can." Keep your eyes on the exalted Man at the Father's right hand, who holds all authority in heaven and on earth. You're never more frightening to the devil than when you look up.

messages.text: Who will be caught up? Not "we who are faithful" or "we who are overcomers," but "we who are alive and remain."
messages.explanation:
Picture a young believer in Thessalonica, one who sometimes wins against temptation and sometimes loses, listening anxiously as Paul's letter is read aloud. "For this we say to you by the word of the Lord, that we who…" Who? The faithful? The watchful? "…we who are alive and remain."

The rapture is the redemption of your body, and your body is redeemed by the same grace that saved your soul: not half grace and half your performance. Live to honour Him, yes. But the Lord is coming to claim what He already purchased, and He paid for all of you.

messages.text: Paul wrote "We shall all be changed" to the most carnal church he ever had: the Corinthians.
messages.explanation:
The Corinthian believers were suing one another, splitting into factions and abusing the Lord's Supper, yet Paul called their bodies temples of the Holy Spirit. And to them he wrote, "We shall not all sleep, but we shall all be changed, in a moment." All. The order of resurrection is "Christ the firstfruits, afterward those who are Christ's at His coming": those who belong to Him.

That isn't a licence to live carelessly; a believer living in sin is a walking civil war. But fear never produced lasting holiness. "Everyone who has this hope in Him purifies himself." It's the blessed hope that cleans you up.

messages.text: "I'm not afraid of the bulldozers. He said that when my new house was ready, he'd come for me himself."
messages.explanation:
A landowner bought a large estate for development, with an old woman's run-down cottage in the middle of it. He visited her personally and promised her a much better house, with running water and help close by: "When it's ready, I'll come and get you myself." Months later, the bulldozers lined up outside her door. A worker asked if she was frightened. "No," she said. "He told me he's coming for me." And he did.

As you watch the world's troubles gather, remember who promised, "I go to prepare a place for you… I will come again and receive you to Myself." The worst hasn't happened yet, and He's coming for you first.

messages.text: Luke begins with a priest who came out of the temple unable to bless. It ends with our High Priest ascending with His hands raised in blessing.
messages.explanation:
In Luke 1, the people waited outside while Zacharias burned incense in the temple, wondering why he was taking so long. When he finally came out, he'd been struck mute and couldn't pronounce the priestly blessing. Nothing is sadder than a priest who can't bless.

Luke's Gospel closes with Jesus lifting His hands to bless His disciples, "and while He blessed them, He was parted from them." Now He has gone into the true Holy Place, and "to those who eagerly wait for Him He will appear a second time." Waiting isn't a condition you must meet; it's what His people naturally do while their Priest is inside. And when He comes out, He'll come out blessing.

messages.text: The Old Testament ends with the Sun of Righteousness. The New ends with the Bright and Morning Star, which rises before the sun.
messages.explanation:
The last chapter of the Old Testament promises Israel that "the Sun of Righteousness shall arise with healing in His wings." The last chapter of the Bible has Jesus calling Himself "the Bright and Morning Star." The morning star appears in the dark, before the dawn; only later does the sun rise for the day.

That's a picture of the two stages of His coming: first for His church, quietly and suddenly, before the day of judgment; then in full brightness for Israel and the world. Jesus' last words in Scripture are "Surely I am coming quickly," and the church answers, "Even so, come, Lord Jesus!"

messages.text: Prayer puts God in His place as the Giver, and you in yours as the receiver.
messages.explanation:
Some people think of prayer as hard work, a way of earning God's attention. But prayer is simply coming to the One who loves to give and holding out your hands. "You do not have because you do not ask."

God already knows what you need, yet He delights to be asked, the way a father loves his child's requests. So pray for protection, for your children, for wisdom and provision, even for small things. Nothing is too big for Him, and nothing is too small to bring.

messages.text: Melchizedek's first words to Abraham were a blessing. His is a priesthood of blessing only, and Jesus is a priest for ever in his order.
messages.explanation:
Melchizedek, king of Salem and priest of God Most High, came out to meet Abraham with bread and wine, and said, "Blessed be Abram of God Most High." Under the law, the Levitical priests pronounced both blessings and curses. Melchizedek pronounced only blessing.

"The Lord has sworn and will not relent: 'You are a priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek.'" Jesus' priestly ministry for you today isn't after the order of Aaron, but of Melchizedek: King of righteousness, King of peace, whose word over you is blessing.

messages.text: Communion proclaims the Lord's death until He comes. Hebrews says the tithe is a witness that He lives.
messages.explanation:
"Here mortal men receive tithes, but there He receives them, of whom it is witnessed that He lives." The Levitical priests who received tithes in the temple all died. But the One Melchizedek pictures receives them in heaven, and He lives by the power of an endless life.

Abraham met Melchizedek with his hands full, and so did Melchizedek: one brought bread and wine, the other a tenth of the spoils. Salvation is coming to God with empty hands; worship is coming to Him with full ones. When you give, give with a sense of His love, thanking Him for all He's given you.

messages.text: When Jacob saw the wagons Joseph had sent, his spirit revived, and he was called Israel again.
messages.explanation:
For years Jacob grieved over Joseph, believing he was dead. When his sons came home saying, "Joseph is still alive, and he is governor over all the land of Egypt," his heart went numb: he couldn't believe it. But when he heard Joseph's words and saw the wagons Joseph had sent to carry him, "the spirit of Jacob their father revived."

The very next verse calls him Israel: "It is enough. Joseph my son is still alive." The good things God puts in your life are wagons from Someone who is alive and reigning. Let them strengthen your faith, and let others see them too.

messages.text: Abraham's servant took ten camels, "for all his master's goods were in his hand." In Scripture, ten stands for the whole.
messages.explanation:
How could all of Abraham's great wealth be in one servant's hand? Because the ten camels represented it all. Likewise, Joseph couldn't send the whole land of Egypt to his father, so he sent ten donkeys "loaded with the good things of Egypt" as a token of it all. Ten commandments represent the whole law; break one and you've broken all.

That's the principle Paul draws on: "If the firstfruit is holy, the lump is also holy." When the first tenth is set apart to the Lord, the rest is sanctified too. It's not that God needs your money; it's that He wants to bless all of it.

messages.text: The first time "tithe" appears in the Bible, "rich" appears in the same chapter. Abraham refused to let Sodom say, "I made Abram rich."
messages.explanation:
Right after Abraham gave Melchizedek a tenth of everything, the king of Sodom offered him all the goods he had recovered. Abraham refused: "I will take nothing, from a thread to a sandal strap… lest you should say, 'I have made Abram rich.'"

Abraham knew where his blessing came from, and he wasn't going to give that credit to anyone else. The God who received his tithe was the God who would make him rich. Your provision doesn't depend on the world's favours or the world's economy, but on the One who blesses you.

messages.text: Under grace, you don't have to give. You get to.
messages.explanation:
Abraham tithed to Melchizedek long before the law of Moses was given; it was a response of faith, not a commandment. Jesus told the Pharisees that justice and the love of God came first, "without leaving the others undone." Love is the motive; giving is its natural expression.

"Do not forget to do good and to share, for with such sacrifices God is well pleased." If God can be grieved, He can also be gladdened, and a generous heart gladdens Him. Give not out of fear or pride, but because you've seen how much He loves you.

messages.text: Melchizedek is "first King of righteousness, and after that King of peace." Peace always follows righteousness.
messages.explanation:
When the Holy Spirit translates a name for us, He wants us to notice it. Melchizedek means "king of righteousness," and king of Salem means "king of peace," in that order. Just as a champion masters something and can pass it on, Jesus is the King of righteousness: the only One who has it and can give it.

"The work of righteousness will be peace, and the effect of righteousness, quietness and assurance forever." Rather than spreading your faith thin over every problem, use it each morning to believe you are righteous in Christ. Your thoughts and feelings will argue otherwise, but seek His righteousness first and peace will follow.

messages.text: In Hebrew, shalem (wholeness, peace) also means payment. Your shalom was paid for.
messages.explanation:
Salem, from shalem, is the root of shalom: peace, wholeness, completeness. Yet in modern Hebrew, "Ani meshalem" means "I'm paying." The same word means both, because there is no wholeness without a payment. Jesus paid at the cross for the peace you now enjoy.

When the Shunammite woman's son had died and Elisha's servant asked, "Is it well with the child?" she answered with a single word, "Shalom," and the boy was raised. To most people shalom is just a greeting. To you, it's a peace that has been fully paid for, for you and your family.

messages.text: Right after Abraham's greatest victory, the king of Sodom came out to meet him. So did Melchizedek, with bread and wine.
messages.explanation:
Abraham had just chased four kings over 150 miles with 318 servants and won. Exhausted and responsible for all the people he'd rescued, he was met by the king of Sodom, whose name means "son of evil." The enemy often shows up right after a great victory, when you feel strongest and are least likely to pray.

But Melchizedek came too, down into the King's Valley, the Kidron, whose name comes from the word for darkness. It's the same valley where Jesus would later shed His blood in Gethsemane. In your darkest hour, the King of peace comes down to meet you, carrying bread and wine.

messages.text: Normally you bring gifts to a king. This King came out bringing gifts to you.
messages.explanation:
When you visit royalty, you bring something: flowers, a gift. Kings don't usually give; they receive. But Melchizedek, king and priest of God Most High, came out to Abraham with bread and wine to refresh him, and his first word was "Blessed."

That's the order of your High Priest's ministry. He gives first and blesses first. Abraham responded with a tenth of everything, but only after he'd been fed and blessed. Your worship and generosity are a response to a King who came to serve you.

messages.text: "Give me the people; keep the goods." The enemy doesn't mind you being rich, as long as he gets your family.
messages.explanation:
Melchizedek said, "Blessed be Abram." The king of Sodom said, "Give me the persons, and take the goods for yourself." One king gives; the other demands. And what the enemy wanted wasn't money; it was souls. Plenty of people have traded their children and their relationships for wealth.

Abraham answered with the very words he'd just heard from Melchizedek: "I have raised my hand to the Lord, God Most High, Possessor of heaven and earth." Time in the presence of your High Priest puts the right words in your mouth for when temptation comes. Money is for loving people, never the other way round.

messages.text: In John 6:54, "eats" is trogo: to crunch or chew. Jesus wasn't only speaking figuratively; He was pointing to the bread you hold in your hand.
messages.explanation:
Earlier in John 6, Jesus uses the general word for eating, which can describe believing in Him and receiving eternal life. But then He switches to trogo, a word for crunching, like nuts: "Whoever eats My flesh and drinks My blood has eternal life." And He says His flesh is given "for the life of the world": zoe, the life that made Adam a living being, and that brings health to every part that's withering.

"He who eats Me will live because of Me." The bread and cup aren't magic, and they don't turn into literal flesh and blood. But received with revelation, they release the virtue of His broken body into yours. Keep taking your medicine, and take Communion too.

messages.text: Bread is beaten and kneaded; wine is trodden underfoot. He was crushed so He could feed you.
messages.explanation:
To make bread, wheat is threshed, ground, mixed with water and pounded by hand. To make wine, grapes are trampled underfoot and left to ferment. From Gethsemane onwards, Jesus was struck, punched and trodden on, so that He could become bread and wine for you.

When you take Communion, don't take it as a ritual or a charm. The word for "gave thanks" is eucharisteo, from good and grace: be mindful of His favours. Remember what He went through, receive what it bought, and thank Him.

messages.text: God described creation in one chapter. He spent seven chapters describing the tabernacle, a picture of His Son and redemption.
messages.explanation:
The whole universe gets a single chapter in Genesis. But when Moses went up Sinai for forty days and nights, God spent seven chapters, Exodus 25 to 31, describing the ark, the table, the lampstand, the altars, the priest's garments: every one of them a picture of Jesus and His work.

And notice when Moses received the tablets of stone: "at the end of forty days and forty nights." The law came on the last day. For the forty days before that, God's heart was full of His Son. If you want to see what delights God most, look at Jesus.

messages.text: Blue, purple, scarlet: always in that order. Heaven's blue and earth's red meet in the purple of a King.
messages.explanation:
Blue is the colour of heaven: Jesus came from above, and His words and touch carried something heavenly. Scarlet speaks of blood and suffering, of Adam (whose name means red), and of Israel's kings, which is why the soldiers mocked Jesus in a scarlet robe as "King of the Jews." Purple was the colour of Gentile emperors.

Set blue and red side by side and they clash. Put purple between them and the eye rests. And purple is what you get when you blend blue and red. In Jesus, heaven and earth meet in one Person: fully God, fully man, and King of kings.

messages.text: In Jesus' empty tomb, two angels sat at the head and the feet, just like the two cherubim facing each other over the mercy seat.
messages.explanation:
The cherubim on the ark guarded God's holiness; the first cherubim in Scripture held a flaming sword at Eden's gate. Yet on the ark they faced each other, looking down at the mercy seat, where the high priest sprinkled blood once a year. Seeing the blood, they were satisfied: judgment had been carried out.

On resurrection morning, Mary looked into the tomb and saw two angels in white, "one at the head and the other at the feet, where the body of Jesus had lain." The real Mercy Seat. And they were sitting, because the work was finished. God now speaks to you from the mercy seat, not the judgment seat.

messages.text: Every time you come to God, He never says, "You again?"
messages.explanation:
In the tabernacle, twelve loaves, one for each tribe, sat on a golden table before the Lord. It was His bread, His table. God finds His satisfaction in His people coming near to Him. After Jesus had spent time with a broken woman at a well, He told His disciples, "I have food to eat of which you do not know." Blessing her had fed Him.

The table had a golden rim, a crown, all around it, so nothing could fall off. You don't wear out God's welcome by coming too often or asking too much. Heaven is full of unclaimed blessings. Come.

messages.text: God described the ark, table and lampstand first, but held back the altar of incense until after the high priest. No priest, no intercession.
messages.explanation:
In the holy place stood three pieces of furniture: the table of showbread, the lampstand and the golden altar of incense. When God described the tabernacle to Moses, He covered the first two right after the ark, then moved on to curtains, the high priest's garments and the priests' consecration. Only in chapter 30 did He mention the altar of incense.

The incense rose to God as fragrant intercession, and there's no intercession without a priest to offer it. Today Jesus is that High Priest, and "He always lives to make intercession" for you, presenting you to the Father as a sweet fragrance.

messages.text: The burnt offering was killed on the north side of the altar, the direction Israel's invaders always came from.
messages.explanation:
"He shall kill it on the north side of the altar before the Lord." In Israel's geography, enemies and destructive winds came from the north; "out of the north calamity shall break forth." God placed the death of the Lamb right where trouble comes in.

Whatever your need, start at the cross. He became poor so you could be rich. He bore your sicknesses and carried your pains. He was forsaken by lover and friend so you would never be alone. Even when the Shepherd was struck and His sheep scattered, it was so yours would stay together. Every need was met there.

messages.text: "May He accept your burnt sacrifice." The Hebrew word for accept means to reduce to ashes. Ashes mean the fire has finished.
messages.explanation:
On the east side of the altar, the entrance side, was the place for the ashes. Picture a worshipper who offered a lamb yesterday, then went home and started doubting: "Did I do it right? Are my sins really forgiven?" Next morning, as the sun rose in the east, the first thing its light fell on was the ashes. All that was left of yesterday's lamb: proof the judgment was finished.

The Hebrew word for ashes, deshen, also means fatness, abundance. When you come to God, come by the east gate. Remember the ashes. Your sins aren't merely covered; the fire has burned out on Jesus, and there's abundance in the finished work.

messages.text: Whoever takes the Son gets everything else with Him.
messages.explanation:
A wealthy art collector lost his only son in war, and later commissioned a portrait of him. When the old man died, collectors flocked to the auction for his famous paintings. The first item was the son's portrait. No one bid, except the old family servant, who offered what little he had. The hammer fell, and the auctioneer announced the sale was over: the will said whoever took the son's portrait received the entire collection.

God has done the same. "He who did not spare His own Son… how shall He not with Him also freely give us all things?" Have the Son, and you have everything heaven holds.

messages.text: On the Emmaus road, Jesus kept them from recognising Him so they'd see Him in the Scriptures instead.
messages.explanation:
On His resurrection day, Jesus walked with two discouraged disciples, but "their eyes were restrained, so that they did not know Him." Why not just show them His nail-scarred hands? Instead, "beginning at Moses and all the Prophets, He expounded to them in all the Scriptures the things concerning Himself." Their hearts burned.

If they'd been lifted only by seeing Him in person, every generation after them would be at a disadvantage. But they were lifted by seeing Him in the Word, and you can see Him there too. When you're down, look for Jesus on every page.

messages.text: Elijah didn't plead for Israel. Paul says he "pleads with God against Israel." God's answer was 7,000 faithful he didn't know about.
messages.explanation:
After Mount Carmel, Elijah fled from Jezebel, collapsed under a broom tree and asked to die. God didn't scold him; He let him sleep and sent an angel to feed him, twice. But in the cave at Horeb, Elijah listed Israel's sins and said, "I alone am left." God replied, "I have reserved seven thousand who have not bowed to Baal," and told him to anoint his successor.

When we're burned out, it's easy to recount others' failings and imagine we're the only faithful ones left. God isn't impressed by either. And He wasn't in the wind, the earthquake or the fire, but in a still, small voice.

messages.text: When there was death in the pot, Elisha didn't try to remove it. He added flour.
messages.explanation:
During a famine, Elisha had a stew made for the prophets. One man, wanting to improve it, gathered wild gourds that looked good and sliced them in. As they ate, they cried, "Man of God, there is death in the pot!" Elisha said, "Bring some flour," threw it in, and "there was nothing harmful in the pot."

In this world, a little uncleanness spoils what's clean: a drop of sewage ruins a glass of the purest water. Only Jesus reverses it. When He touched lepers, they became clean; when He stepped into death, death had to leave. Bring Him into the situation.

messages.text: The grain offering was fine flour: smooth, with no coarse grains. In Jesus, no trait ever overpowers another.
messages.explanation:
Four of the five Levitical offerings picture Jesus' death; the grain offering pictures His life. It was fine flour: nothing coarse or uneven. He was truthful but kind, firm without being harsh, a servant washing feet but never servile. Oil was poured on it, as the Spirit led His every word; frankincense rose from it, as every deed pleased the Father.

The cakes were "mixed with oil" and the wafers "anointed with oil." He was conceived by the Holy Spirit in Mary's womb, and at thirty the Spirit came upon Him at the Jordan. When you need something to meditate on, try just two words: fine flour.

messages.text: Your wilderness is His storehouse.
messages.explanation:
In a famine, a man brought Elisha twenty loaves of firstfruits bread. "Shall I set this before a hundred men?" the servant asked. Elisha said, "Thus says the Lord: they shall eat and have some left over," and they did. Jesus did the same, but bigger: over five thousand men fed, with twelve baskets left. And He didn't need to say "Thus says the Lord." He is the Lord.

When the disciples said, "This is a deserted place," they saw a wilderness. Jesus saw a storehouse. God's provision always exceeds the need; in your Father's house there's bread enough and to spare.

messages.text: "We went through fire and through water; but You brought us out to rich fulfilment." Look for the way out: it leads higher than the way in.
messages.explanation:
"You have caused men to ride over our heads." Sometimes, even with God's favour on you, people walk all over you, and it feels like fire and flood. But the psalm doesn't stop there. The word for "rich fulfilment" or "wealthy place" means saturation, overflowing abundance.

The only other place that word appears is Psalm 23: "You prepare a table before me in the presence of my enemies… my cup runs over." The table is set in the middle of the battle, not after it. When the enemy attacks, keep your eyes on the Lord and come to His table. The way out leads somewhere higher than where you came in.

messages.text: Paul's letters never say "our Father in heaven." Just "Abba, Father." You're no longer far away.
messages.explanation:
When Jesus taught His disciples to pray "Our Father in heaven," He hadn't yet died and risen; they were on earth, and the Father was far above. After the resurrection He said, "I am ascending to My Father and your Father, to My God and your God." Then "because you are sons, God sent forth the Spirit of His Son into your hearts, crying out, 'Abba, Father!'"

In the epistles it's simply "Father," "our God and Father," "Abba." At Lazarus' tomb, Jesus didn't look up and say "Father in heaven," but "Father, I thank You that You have heard Me." That's the nearness He has given you. Say "Father," and know you're close.
