messages.explanation:
Under the law, if property went missing and someone said, "This is it" (literally, this is mine), both parties came before God, and "whomever the judges condemn shall pay double to his neighbour." But you can't say "This is mine" if you've been taught that healing, provision or the gifts of the Spirit aren't for today.

When the enemy steals your health, peace or finances, don't condemn yourself as if you're the one who deserves it. Come before the Father as the righteousness of God in Christ and say, "Healing is mine. Peace is mine." Then God condemns the thief, and the thief must restore double.

messages.text: The Hebrew word for "stripes," makkah, is also used for plague. "By His stripes we are healed."
messages.explanation:
The law limited a guilty man's beating to forty stripes. The word, makkah, also means a blow or plague, and Deuteronomy 28's curses use it for "extraordinary plagues… serious and prolonged sicknesses… every sickness and every plague." Jesus wasn't flogged under Jewish limits but by Romans, until "His visage was marred more than any man." He took the stripes the guilty deserved.

The curses of Deuteronomy 28 end with: "you shall be offered for sale… but no one will buy you." But Christ did. "Christ has redeemed us from the curse of the law" (literally bought us out of the slave market) "having become a curse for us."

messages.text: God measured the prodigal by the fatted calf, and the older brother by his own record.
messages.explanation:
The son who rebelled and wasted everything came home to a robe, a ring, sandals and a feast. The son who stayed and boasted, "I never transgressed your commandment at any time," felt like he'd never received anything. Why? The father treated the prodigal according to the sacrifice, the fatted calf, a picture of Jesus. The older son insisted on his own righteousness, so that's what he was measured by.

Whose righteousness are you standing in? If it's Christ's, God treats you as He treats His Son, and nothing is withheld. If it's your own, you'll receive what your record deserves, which isn't much.

messages.text: Jesus filled Peter's boat to sinking first. Then Peter fell at His knees and repented.
messages.explanation:
Peter had fished all night and caught nothing. Jesus told him to let down his nets, and the catch was so great the nets began to break and both boats began to sink. Only then did Peter fall at Jesus' knees: "Depart from me, for I am a sinful man, O Lord!" The goodness came before the repentance.

Sometimes God anoints you or blesses you on a day you know you don't deserve it, perhaps after a quarrel with your spouse. It's not because He approves of the quarrel. It's so you'll know His blessing was never about your performance. And that goodness is exactly what moves you to go home and make things right.

messages.text: "Bringing every thought into captivity to the obedience of Christ": His obedience, not yours.
messages.explanation:
The battle is in the mind. Strongholds are patterns of thinking the enemy has built up over months or years, and they come as "arguments" that sound reasonable. As a teenager trying to force every blasphemous thought to obey, Joseph Prince found that the harder he tried, the worse they got. But Paul doesn't say "make every thought obey Christ." In Greek, obedience is a noun: bring each thought to the obedience of the Christ.

Which obedience? "By one Man's obedience many will be made righteous." When the accuser says you haven't prayed enough, read enough or done enough, don't argue about your obedience. Turn every thought back to His: "His obedience made me righteous."

messages.text: Your emotions are a mirror of your thoughts. If you feel bad, check what you're thinking.
messages.explanation:
Joseph Prince once told his young son, "If you feel bad, it's because you're thinking bad thoughts: that tomorrow won't go well, that you can't do it." But if you think, "Jesus is going with me to school. He'll be my best friend and never leave me," your feelings follow.

Many thought patterns have been there so long you no longer notice them. But your emotions can't lie. Depression, self-loathing and dread always trace back to something you've been believing. Right believing leads to right living, and to right feelings too. Find the thought, and replace it with what God says.

messages.text: Jesus told Ephesus, "I know your works, labour and patience." Missing: the faith, love and hope behind them.
messages.explanation:
It sounds like praise: "I know your works, your labour, your patience." But compare Paul's thanks for the Thessalonians: "your work of faith, labour of love, and patience of hope in our Lord Jesus Christ." Same three words, in the same order. Ephesus had the activity, but not the faith, love and hope that make it holy. Jesus said, "You have left your first love."

Holiness isn't grim duty done with a face soured by lemon juice. Work without faith is dead work. Labour without love is a clanging cymbal. Patience without hope is quiet bitterness. When grace is preached, the work, the labour and the patience come out radiant.

messages.text: Goodness and mercy don't just follow you. They hunt you down, all the days of your life.
messages.explanation:
"Surely goodness and mercy shall follow me all the days of my life." The Hebrew word for follow, radaph, means to pursue, to chase down. Turn one way, and you run into His goodness. Turn the other, and you run into His mercy, His chesed, His covenant favour.

It doesn't say some days or the good days; it says all of them, every day of every week, of every year, until you dwell in the house of the Lord forever. Wake up each morning expecting to be overtaken by His goodness today.

messages.text: "Thus shall the man be blessed." Don't try to make your wife be; focus on being the blessed man.
messages.explanation:
"Your wife shall be like a fruitful vine in the very heart of your house, your children like olive plants all around your table. Behold, thus shall the man be blessed who fears the Lord." Notice the order: this is what the blessed man's home looks like. It isn't his job to nag his wife and push his children into shape. His job is to be the blessed man.

When you're established in God's gift of righteousness, it spills over. A vine in fruit speaks of joy and delight; olive plants speak of anointing, where everything flows smoothly. Stay under His blessing, and watch your family flourish around you.

messages.text: You're parenting even when you're not saying anything. Children pick up your fears.
messages.explanation:
We teach parents about discipline and communication, and those matter. But the biggest factor is the parent. If your children hear you say, "I don't know where this pandemic is going to end," they learn that the world isn't safe. Many childhood fears and phobias are simply learned, and we end up treating the branches while the root is us.

"In righteousness you shall be established; you shall be far from oppression, for you shall not fear." When you're settled in God's love, your children absorb that security without a word being spoken. Watch what you say in front of them, and let them catch your confidence in God.

messages.text: Truth is higher than facts, and truth outlasts facts.
messages.explanation:
Ten spies reported the facts: the giants were real and the walls were high. Joshua and Caleb didn't deny any of it, but they brought God into the picture: "The Lord is with us. Do not fear them… they are our bread." Their faith-filled words came true. The others never entered the land.

It may be a fact that your body is in pain, or that the diagnosis is real. But "by His stripes you were healed" is truth, and truth outlasts facts. Many who once had a condition are free of it today; the fact didn't last, but the truth did. Acknowledge the facts, then speak the truth over them.

messages.text: Under the law, Israel was nepios: an infant ruled by guardians. In Christ you've had your coming-of-age as a full son.
messages.explanation:
"The heir, as long as he is a child, does not differ at all from a slave, though he is master of all, but is under guardians and stewards until the time appointed by the father." The word for child, nepios, means an infant or minor. Rules like "Don't touch the knives" are right for toddlers, but insulting to adults. The law was a paidagogos, a child-minder, "until Christ came."

Then God sent His Son "to redeem those who were under the law, that we might receive the adoption as sons": huiothesia, son-placement, the ceremony where a father declares his child a grown son and heir. Galatians isn't describing gradual growth; it's your status. "You are no longer a slave but a son."

messages.text: God promised Abraham he'd be "heir of the world." Heirs of that promise can't be always sick and always broke.
messages.explanation:
"The promise that he would be the heir of the world was not to Abraham or to his seed through the law, but through the righteousness of faith." The word for world, kosmos, speaks of an ordered, beautiful arrangement, with its riches and influence. And "if you are Christ's, then you are Abraham's seed, and heirs according to the promise."

It's hard to inherit the world flat on your back. Healing and provision are lesser blessings, all included in the greater one. So why do so many believers live without them? "If those who are of the law are heirs, faith is made void and the promise made of no effect." The inheritance comes through the righteousness of faith, never by trying harder at the law.

messages.text: Because Abraham didn't withhold his son, God had covenant ground to give His own.
messages.explanation:
God gave Adam dominion, and Adam handed it to Satan. God couldn't simply snatch it back; He had to do it righteously. So He cut a covenant with a man, Abraham. But could a mortal man keep his side? The test came on Mount Moriah. Abraham raised the knife over Isaac, and God stopped him: "Now I know that you fear God, since you have not withheld your son, your only son."

In a covenant, what one partner gives, the other gives too. Abraham's willingness opened the way, legally and righteously, for God to give His own Son. "He who did not spare His own Son, but delivered Him up for us all, how shall He not with Him also freely give us all things?"

messages.text: Teach your child identity, not just rules: "You're a Jesus boy. A Jesus boy tells the truth."
messages.explanation:
People ask how we'll raise moral children without drilling them in the Ten Commandments. Most adults who insist on them can't even recite them. Yet small children can easily learn John 3:16. There's grace there.

Instead of "Thou shalt not," speak to who they are: "You're a Jesus boy. A Jesus boy doesn't lie. A Jesus boy protects others; he doesn't bully them." Behaviour flows from identity. "Be imitators of God as dear children." Children who know they're dearly loved naturally want to be like their Father.

messages.text: In Revelation, only the redeemed address God as "You." The angels speak of Him in the third person.
messages.explanation:
The twenty-four elders sing, "You are worthy… for You were slain, and have redeemed us to God by Your blood… and have made us kings and priests." No angel could sing that; angels were never redeemed. When the myriads of angels join in, the song shifts: "Worthy is the Lamb who was slain." Heaven has order, and closest to the throne are the redeemed.

So don't come to God as a servant hovering at a distance. "You did not receive the spirit of bondage again to fear, but the Spirit of adoption by whom we cry out, 'Abba, Father.'" The Spirit of truth can't bear witness to a lie, and approaching as a slave is one. Come close; He longs to hear your voice.

messages.text: The shepherd's rod is for wolves. The crook on his staff is for sheep that fall.
messages.explanation:
"Your rod and Your staff, they comfort me." Some teach that a shepherd breaks the leg of a lamb that keeps wandering, then carries it until it learns. You won't find that in Psalm 23: no "He breaks my legs." In Israel the rod was a weapon against lions and wolves, or thrown ahead of a sheep to turn it from a ravine, never to beat it.

And the staff has a crook at the end precisely because the shepherd expects his sheep to stumble. When you fall, He doesn't strike you; He hooks you gently and lifts you back. That's why His rod and staff are a comfort, not a threat.

messages.text: "Ought not this woman, being a daughter of Abraham, be loosed?" Once you believe, you qualify.
messages.explanation:
A woman had been bent double for eighteen years. Jesus laid hands on her, and she stood straight; the first face she saw was His. The synagogue ruler complained, "There are six days on which men ought to work." His "ought" was about labour. Jesus answered with a different "ought": "Ought not this woman, being a daughter of Abraham, whom Satan has bound… be loosed from this bond?"

Not everyone in that synagogue was a child of Abraham in that sense. When she believed in Jesus, she became one, and from that moment, Jesus couldn't leave her bound a minute longer. He said the same of Zacchaeus: "Today salvation has come to this house, because he also is a son of Abraham." If you believe, so are you.

messages.text: Faith is having a good opinion of God. Sarah "judged Him faithful who had promised."
messages.explanation:
"Without faith it is impossible to please Him." But what does faith look like in everyday life? It's thinking the best of God. Sarah received strength to conceive at ninety "because she judged Him faithful who had promised." She didn't have to work up her own faith; she rested on His faithfulness. Abraham "did not consider his own body, already dead… but was strengthened in faith, giving glory to God."

In the New Testament, the word for glory, doxa, carries the idea of a good opinion. To give God glory is to hold the highest view of Him. When you don't understand what's happening, say it anyway: "God is faithful. He's for me, not against me."

messages.text: God said, "Of every tree you may freely eat." The serpent made Him sound stingy, and Eve dropped the word "freely."
messages.explanation:
The first temptation was an attack on God's generosity. "Has God indeed said, 'You shall not eat of every tree of the garden'?" In fact, He'd said the opposite: every tree, freely, except one. Eve's reply shows the poison working: "We may eat the fruit of the trees" ("freely" is gone), and "you shall not… touch it" (added). Take away from His word, add rules to it, and soon you have a bad opinion of God.

The enemy still whispers that God is holding out on you. But He "gives us richly all things to enjoy." He's only against what would destroy you, like a parent shouting to a child near a cliff edge. "At Your right hand are pleasures forevermore."

messages.text: Zechariah asked, "How shall I know this?" Mary asked, "How can this be?" One doubted God's word; the other asked about His method.
messages.explanation:
Gabriel brought good news to two people. Elderly Zechariah answered, "How shall I know this? For I am an old man." In other words: how can I be sure you're telling the truth? He was left unable to speak until John was born, perhaps so his unbelief wouldn't undo the promise. Young Mary asked, "How can this be, since I do not know a man?" She wasn't doubting; she was asking how.

Gabriel answered her: "The Holy Spirit will come upon you… For with God nothing will be impossible." And she said, "Let it be to me according to your word." That's the response God loves. When you hear His promise of healing or provision, don't ask for proof. Say, "Be it unto me."

messages.text: Every morning, look in the mirror and say: "You are highly favoured."
messages.explanation:
Gabriel greeted Mary, "Rejoice, highly favoured one, the Lord is with you; blessed are you among women." The Greek word for highly favoured, charitoo, appears only one other time in the New Testament: "to the praise of the glory of His grace, by which He made us accepted (highly favoured) in the Beloved." It's said of you.

So say it over yourself every morning and before you sleep: "I'm highly favoured. I'm blessed among men, among women." Not above others, but standing out among them. And notice what heaven said next: "Do not be afraid, for you have found favour with God." When bad news comes, remind yourself of that.

messages.text: In Hebrew, "Amen" is the root of the word for believe. And Jesus is called "the Amen."
messages.explanation:
"Abraham believed in the Lord, and He accounted it to him for righteousness." The Hebrew word for believed is from the same root as amen. So when you say amen, you're saying, "I believe it. So be it. It's certain." And in Revelation, Jesus calls Himself "the Amen, the Faithful and True Witness."

Paul said his preaching wasn't "Yes and No," sometimes God heals, sometimes He doesn't. "For all the promises of God in Him are Yes, and in Him Amen, to the glory of God through us." God says yes; you say amen; God gets the glory, and you get the promise. Don't shrug and say, "If it happens, it happens." Say amen.

messages.text: At the sound of Mary's voice, the baby leapt in Elizabeth's womb. Your words can awaken someone's dormant dream.
messages.explanation:
When Mary arrived and greeted her, Elizabeth said, "As soon as the voice of your greeting sounded in my ears, the babe leaped in my womb for joy. Blessed is she who believed, for there will be a fulfilment of those things which were told her from the Lord."

The words you speak carry life. A dream that seems barren, or a promise that feels dormant in someone, can leap with new life when they hear God's word from your mouth. Speak blessing over your spouse, your children, your work. Don't say, "He'll never change." Say, "He'll be saved, in Jesus' name." God spoke light into darkness; you're made in His image.

messages.text: "If God is for us, who can be against us?" The Greek also reads: what can be against us?
messages.explanation:
The little Greek word tis can mean who or what. So it's not only that no person can stand against you; no circumstance can either. The retrenchment, the bad report, the painful breakup: none of them are good in themselves, but "all things work together for good to those who love God." The word is sunergeo, synergy: things combining to produce good.

You can only see one step ahead; God sees the end from the beginning. Perhaps a better job is waiting that you'd never have reached by holding on to this one. Keep a good opinion of Him, and trust Him for the good He's working out.

messages.text: "The Lord your God will set you high above all nations… and all these blessings shall come upon you." Position comes before blessing.
messages.explanation:
Before Deuteronomy 28 lists a single blessing, it states a position: God sets His people high above. Only then do the blessings "come upon you and overtake you." That's a picture of where you are in Christ. "Blessed be the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, who has blessed us with every spiritual blessing in the heavenly places in Christ."

So don't live earthbound, as if you're limited to what's in your bank account or what your boss decides to pay you. You're seated with Christ, far above every name that is named. Take your place there, and let the blessings find you.

messages.text: Peter put the mourners out, knelt down and prayed, and only then turned to the body and said, "Tabitha, arise."
messages.explanation:
Tabitha, a woman full of good works, died in Joppa, whose name means beautiful: death had come into a place of beauty. The widows crowded around Peter, weeping and showing the garments she'd made, as if her good deeds might earn a miracle. But healing is a grace gift, never wages. Peter did what he'd seen Jesus do in Jairus' house: "Peter put them all out, and knelt down and prayed. And turning to the body he said, 'Tabitha, arise.'"

When death touches your situation, follow the same order. Put out the negative voices, the endless bad news and the doubting talk. Pray. Then turn to the situation and speak to it in Jesus' name. "It became known throughout all Joppa, and many believed on the Lord."

messages.text: Both Tabitha and the Shunammite's son were laid in an upper room. When death strikes, bring it into the place of anointing.
messages.explanation:
The Shunammite woman built a small room on her roof for Elisha. When her miracle son died, she didn't wail or make funeral plans. She carried him up, laid him on the man of God's bed, shut the door, and went to find Elisha. Asked, "Is it well with the child?" she answered, "It is well." Shalom. Not a lie, but faith that it shall be well.

When something precious seems to be dying, whether a child drifting, a marriage or your health, expose it to the anointing. Keep hearing the Word. Surround your children with it: play it in the car, and use your God-given authority in your home lovingly. The child was raised between the anointing above and the anointing beneath.

messages.text: "He who would love life and see good days, let him refrain his tongue from evil."
messages.explanation:
Is it biblical to want good days? Peter says so, and tells you where to start: your tongue. You can't author fear and doom in your speech and expect beautiful days to follow.

Interestingly, the Hebrew word for pestilence in Psalm 91, dever, shares its letters with davar, word. There's a link between what we say and what we experience. If you want to love life in the coming year, watch your words. Speak blessing over your body, your family and your future.

messages.text: When his own brother mocked him, David "turned from him." Learn to turn away from the naysayers.
messages.explanation:
As David asked about Goliath, his eldest brother Eliab burned with anger: "I know your pride and the insolence of your heart." David didn't stay to argue. "What have I done now? Is there not a cause?" Then "he turned from him toward another," and kept moving toward his giant.

You can't see good days while marinating in negativity. Turn away from critics who question your motives. Turn off the drama that's fearful from start to finish. Stop scrolling from one piece of bad news to the next. Turn your face toward what God has said.

messages.text: Peter stayed "many days in Joppa with Simon, a tanner." Two Simons, "hearing," in the place called "beautiful."
messages.explanation:
The chapter ends with this quiet detail: Peter stayed many days in Joppa, the beautiful place, at the house of Simon the tanner. Simon comes from shema, to hear, and here there are two of them: Simon Peter and Simon the tanner. Hearing and hearing. A tanner works with hides, turning raw flesh into leather.

It pictures the hearing that brings many beautiful days: not a hearing of the flesh, in one ear and out the other, but hearing mixed with faith. Israel heard God's word in the wilderness, "but the word which they heard did not profit them, not being mixed with faith." As you hear, say in your heart, "This is for me." Faith comes by hearing, and hearing.

messages.text: "Where there is no vision (chazon), the people perish." Before God does anything, He gives a vision.
messages.explanation:
In Samuel's childhood, "the word of the Lord was rare in those days; there was no widespread revelation." The word for vision there, chazon, is the same one in Proverbs: "Where there is no revelation, the people cast off restraint." People don't perish for lack of money or connections, but for lack of a God-given picture of the future.

That's why the enemy works so hard to fill your mind with dark images. He robs your vision before he robs you. But God is restoring hope to His people: a confident expectation of good. Ask Him for His vision for your family, your health and your work, and let it shape how you face each day.

messages.text: "The word of the Lord came to Abram in a vision: 'I am your shield.'" Abram answered, "Seeing I go childless…"
messages.explanation:
God's word came to Abram as a picture: a shield, and an exceedingly great reward. But Abram's inner picture hadn't changed: "Lord God, what will You give me, seeing I go childless?" So God took him outside and said, "Look now toward heaven, and count the stars… So shall your descendants be." Night after night, the stars filled his heart with a new picture. "And he believed in the Lord."

God often has to change the vision inside before the outside changes. What do you see when you think of your future: "Seeing I've been retrenched… seeing the doctor said…"? Let God replace that picture with His.

messages.text: "Out of the abundance of the heart the mouth speaks." Change the pictures in your heart, and your words will follow.
messages.explanation:
"A good man out of the good treasure of his heart brings forth good." We often focus on making our mouths say the right things, but if our hearts still hold images of fear, the words feel hollow and we feel like hypocrites. The mouth only overflows with what fills the heart.

That's why God speaks in pictures: a tree by rivers of water whose leaf doesn't wither, a shield, a land as far as you can see. Fill your heart with what God shows you. "Keep your heart with all diligence, for out of it spring the issues of life." Guard what you let in, and good things will come out.

messages.text: "What God has cleansed you must not call common." Stop labelling people. Every one of them is someone Christ died for.
messages.explanation:
On a Joppa rooftop at noon, Peter saw a sheet full of animals that were unclean under the law, and heard, "Rise, Peter; kill and eat." When he refused, the voice said, "What God has cleansed you must not call common." It happened three times. Then messengers from a Gentile centurion arrived, and Peter understood: "God has shown me that I should not call any man common or unclean."

We're quick to put people into categories and dismiss whole groups. But in God's eyes there's one category of people outside Christ: sinners He loves. Laws and labels never change a heart; the gospel does. Fellowship with believers, yes, but don't keep your distance from those who need Jesus.

messages.text: "That the eyes of your heart may be enlightened." The Spirit of wisdom works by flooding your heart's eyes with light.
messages.explanation:
Paul prays for believers who already have the Holy Spirit, that God "may give you the spirit of wisdom and revelation in the knowledge of Him, the eyes of your understanding being enlightened." The heart has eyes. The word enlightened, photizo (as in photo), means flooded with light.

When God filled Bezalel "with the Spirit of God, in wisdom, in understanding," he could design the ark and the golden lampstand. That's how wisdom feels: "I see it! Now I know what to do." Pray this prayer daily over yourself and your children, and expect to see what others miss: in your work, your parenting and your walk with God.

messages.text: Cornelius wasn't saved yet, but his prayers rose "for a memorial before God." God always finds the one reaching for Him.
messages.explanation:
Cornelius was a Roman soldier who gave generously and prayed to God always, though he hadn't yet heard the gospel. An angel told him, "Your prayers and your alms have come up for a memorial before God," and sent him to find Peter, "who will tell you words by which you and all your household will be saved." He gathered his relatives and close friends to hear, and while Peter was still speaking, the Holy Spirit fell on them all.

People ask, "What about those who never hear about Jesus?" Cornelius is the answer: if a heart cries out for God, God will send the word. And you can be like him, inviting family and friends to hear.

messages.text: Scripture speaks of "the evil day" (singular) and "good days" (plural).
messages.explanation:
"Take up the whole armour of God, that you may be able to withstand in the evil day." Day, singular. But "he who would love life and see good days": plural. Hard seasons come, but they're brief compared to the good ones God has planned.

It's scriptural to expect good days. Elihu, who spoke for God in the book of Job, said that those who hear and serve Him "shall spend their days in prosperity, and their years in pleasures." Don't let anyone talk you out of expecting a year with many beautiful days.

messages.text: "The Son can do nothing of Himself, but what He sees the Father do." Jesus ministered from what He saw.
messages.explanation:
At the pool of Bethesda lay "a great multitude of sick people," yet Jesus healed one man, who'd been ill for thirty-eight years. Healing is for all, and everyone who touched Him was made well. But when He went to someone on His own initiative, He followed what the Father showed Him. "Most assuredly, I say to you, the Son can do nothing of Himself, but what He sees the Father do."

Jesus lived as a man anointed by the Spirit, and He's our pattern. "For the Father loves the Son, and shows Him all things that He Himself does; and He will show Him greater works than these, that you may marvel." Ask your Father to show you too, and expect to marvel this year.

messages.text: Habakkuk said, "I will watch to see what He will say to me." God answered, "Write the vision and make it plain."
messages.explanation:
Habakkuk was troubled by the violence and injustice around him: "O Lord, how long shall I cry, and You will not hear?" Instead of stewing, he positioned himself: "I will stand my watch… and watch to see what He will say to me." Not "hear": see. And God answered: "Write the vision and make it plain on tablets, that he may run who reads it. For the vision is yet for an appointed time… though it tarries, wait for it."

Set aside time away from the noise, with a notebook ready. That's an act of faith. Write down what He shows you: a verse, a phrase, a picture. Years later, those pages will build your faith. Run with what you've seen.

messages.text: "All the land which you see I give to you." The provision is in the vision.
messages.explanation:
After Lot separated from him, God told Abram, "Lift your eyes now and look… northward, southward, eastward, and westward; for all the land which you see I give to you and your descendants forever." What he saw, he received. Even the word provision contains vision.

A vision from God isn't bound by time. He shows you the end as though it's already done, and you can enjoy it now while you wait for it to manifest. Moses "endured as seeing Him who is invisible," and at 120 his eyes weren't dim nor his strength gone. See Jesus first; in Him, everything else is secured.

messages.text: Blinded Saul was praying, and saw a vision of a man named Ananias, "grace of God." Grace was the first face he saw.
messages.explanation:
After meeting the risen Jesus on the Damascus road, Saul was blind for three days. The Lord told a disciple named Ananias, "Behold, he is praying. And in a vision he has seen a man named Ananias coming in and putting his hand on him, so that he might receive his sight." Ananias, Hananiah in Hebrew, means "the Lord is gracious."

While his physical eyes were closed, Saul's heart saw grace coming. And when the scales fell, the first person he saw was "grace of God," the theme of his whole life's message. Notice that Peter, Cornelius and Paul all received visions while praying. Pray, and watch.

messages.text: See your disease on Jesus' body on the cross. From that moment, it begins to wither from the roots.
messages.explanation:
When Israel was bitten by serpents, they were told to look at the bronze serpent on the pole, not at their wounds. "As Moses lifted up the serpent in the wilderness, even so must the Son of Man be lifted up." A loving parent would take their child's sickness if they could. Jesus did: "Surely He has borne our griefs and carried our sorrows."

So picture it: that growth, that pressure, that condition, on His body on the cross, not yours. When Jesus cursed the fig tree, it still looked green that day, but the next morning it was "dried up from the roots." Things may look the same at first. Keep seeing it on Him.

messages.text: Grace is attracted to your weaknesses, not your highlight reel.
messages.explanation:
We post our best moments and hide our weak ones, then scroll through everyone else's highlights and feel our lives are miserable by comparison. But Jesus said, "My grace is sufficient for you, for My strength is made perfect in weakness."

His power can't flow through the parts where you're relying on your own strength. It flows through the cracks. That's why Paul could say, "When I am weak, then I am strong." If you have a lot of weaknesses, you're a candidate for a lot of His power.

messages.text: "Your young men shall see visions, your old men shall dream dreams": pictures are the language of the Spirit.
messages.explanation:
On the day of Pentecost, Peter announced, "This is what was spoken by the prophet Joel… I will pour out of My Spirit on all flesh… your young men shall see visions, your old men shall dream dreams." A dream is a picture while you sleep; a vision is a picture while you're awake. Both are the Spirit's language, and they're for the new covenant, for these last days.

Yes, false visions exist. But a bride and groom don't spend their wedding studying grounds for divorce. Don't let fear of the counterfeit rob you of the real. When God fills you with His Spirit, expect Him to speak in pictures, and learn His language.

messages.text: Daniel "saw a dream and visions of his head while on his bed. Then he wrote down the dream."
messages.explanation:
We imagine visions must be spectacular: an angel appearing, the room glowing, everyone present seeing it too. But Daniel, to whom God gave "understanding in all visions and dreams," received many of his while lying in bed, as thoughts came to his mind. Even Paul's companions on the Damascus road didn't see what he saw.

God said, "If there is a prophet among you, I, the Lord, make Myself known to him in a vision; I speak to him in a dream." What was once reserved for prophets is now the inheritance of every believer. When you pray, expect gentle pictures to rise from within. Don't dismiss them. Write them down, and test them against the Word later.

messages.text: God never makes your mind passive and takes you over. He works with your will, never around it.
messages.explanation:
The occult has "automatic writing": blank the mind, surrender the will, and let a spirit move the pen. The devil always copies God's ways, with one difference: God never overrides your choice. Even tongues require you to speak. You stay fully yourself, in your right mind, a co-worker with God.

So ask Him in faith: "How do You see my marriage? My work? Me?" Pray in the Spirit, then watch and listen, and write down what comes. A new covenant word will always lead to "edification and exhortation and comfort." Even a warning from God comes with His peace and a way forward. Fearful pictures that leave you crushed aren't from Him; bind them in Jesus' name.

messages.text: The blessed man "will not see when heat comes." The cursed man "shall not see when good comes."
messages.explanation:
Jeremiah paints two pictures. The one who trusts in the Lord "shall be like a tree planted by the waters… and will not fear when heat comes; but her leaf will be green, and will not be anxious in the year of drought." The heat still comes, but he isn't fixed on it. The man who trusts in man "shall be like a shrub in the desert, and shall not see when good comes." Good comes, but he can't see it.

Some people can find a problem in every solution, a hidden motive behind every kindness, a fault in every spouse. Choose to look for the good: in your family, your colleagues, even this season. That isn't denying reality; it's seeing the reality the cursed man misses.

messages.text: "The righteous shall flourish like a palm tree, grow like a cedar… they shall still bear fruit in old age; they shall be fresh."
messages.explanation:
God speaks in pictures so they can fill your heart. The date palm stands tall and keeps producing fruit well into its old age. Some cedars are over a thousand years old, still strong, still fragrant. "Those who are planted in the house of the Lord… shall still bear fruit in old age; they shall be fresh and flourishing": the word means luxuriantly green.

And Isaiah adds, "As the days of a tree, so shall be the days of My people." Some olive trees live for two thousand years. Let these be the images you carry of your future: not frailty and decline, but fruitfulness, freshness and strength.

messages.text: "Your children like olive plants around your table." Olive growers renew an old tree with young shoots.
messages.explanation:
God could simply have said, "Your children will be a blessing." Instead He gives a picture to study. An olive tree is useful in every part (fruit, oil, wood, leaves), and it's famous for living very long. When an olive tree grows old, young shoots growing from its base take over and the tree carries on for centuries; some in the Garden of Gethsemane are extremely old.

Children renew our youth. And "your wife shall be like a fruitful vine": the vine gives grapes, and grapes give wine, so she will delight and intoxicate you. If that isn't how things look right now, don't describe your family as they appear. Describe them as God sees them.

messages.text: In Eden, eyes opened by the wrong tree saw nakedness. At Emmaus, eyes opened at the breaking of bread saw Him.
messages.explanation:
God crowned man "with glory and honour," and Adam and Eve lived wrapped in that glory. But they ate from the tree of the knowledge of good and evil, "the eyes of both of them were opened, and they knew that they were naked": they saw their lack and their shame. God had wanted their eyes opened through the tree of life.

On resurrection day, Jesus walked with two disciples, a husband and wife perhaps, just as God once walked with the first couple. At their table "He took bread, blessed and broke it… Then their eyes were opened and they knew Him." The Lord's Supper is your tree of life. Each time you partake, don't see your lack. See Him, and all His supply.

messages.text: Fill your heart with God's pictures, or something else will fill it for you.
messages.explanation:
You were designed to be shaped by pictures. If your heart isn't filled with the images God gives in His Word, a vine, a palm tree, a shield, a table prepared, it won't stay empty. Hours of violence, betrayal and bad news will supply the pictures instead, and then you lie down at night with dread, suspicion and a gloomy view of the future.

Relax with your family and enjoy good things, but guard what you feed your imagination. Spend time in the Word and listening to it. One word from God can change your life, and one picture from Him can replace years of fear.

messages.text: In one English town, squares are painted on the street with names: places people paid for. Jesus paid for your place of favour.
messages.explanation:
In an old English town with a famous yearly parade, squares are painted along the streets, each with a name inside: people who've bought the right to stand there on the day. Nobody pays for a spot and then stays home, satisfied that their name is on it. They come and stand in it.

"Having been justified by faith, we have peace with God… through whom also we have access by faith into this grace in which we stand." Jesus paid for your square on favour ground, and your name is written on it. Don't just know it; possess it. Say, "I'm standing on favour ground. When trouble comes, God turns it around for my good."

messages.text: At the cross, noon became midnight: Christ in a circle of darkness. At the resurrection, He stands in a circle of light, and you're in Him.
messages.explanation:
At His birth, angels filled the night sky so that midnight was like midday. At the cross it was the reverse: "It was about the sixth hour, and there was darkness over all the earth." Picture Christ at the centre of a circle of darkness, bearing every sin, every curse, every judgment that was ours.

Then picture Him risen, at the centre of a circle of light, under God's unclouded favour, without our sins, which were left behind in the tomb. And God "raised us up together." No one imagines Jesus is out of favour with God today. "As He is, so are we in this world."

messages.text: Elisha told the king to strike the ground with the arrows of deliverance. He struck only three times, and won only three victories.
messages.explanation:
On his deathbed, Elisha had King Joash shoot "the arrow of the Lord's deliverance," then said, "Take the arrows… strike the ground." The king struck three times and stopped. "The man of God was angry with him, and said, 'You should have struck five or six times; then you would have struck Syria till you had destroyed it! But now you will strike Syria only three times.'"

Israel "limited the Holy One of Israel." We do the same when we ask small and expect little. God "is able to do exceedingly abundantly above all that we ask or think." If the arrows are His deliverance, keep striking.

messages.text: God doesn't just answer prayer. He over-answers it.
messages.explanation:
As a young man, standing on a staircase in a block of flats, Joseph Prince asked the Lord for a wife from Him, and added, "Make her pretty as well." He says God gave him far more than he asked for.

That's how God gives. Jesus fed five thousand with five loaves and two fish, and twelve baskets were left over. His supply always exceeds the need. Often it's we who refuse, like a friend who insists on paying the bill and robs the giver of his joy. Let Him bless you. Only after you've received from Him can you truly give.

messages.text: Paul wanted "the righteousness which is from God by faith," so "that I may know Him and the power of His resurrection."
messages.explanation:
"That I may be found in Him, not having my own righteousness, which is from the law, but that which is through faith in Christ… that I may know Him and the power of His resurrection." Notice the order. Knowing God intimately, and experiencing His resurrection power, flow from being settled in righteousness as a gift.

The new covenant promises, "They all shall know Me, from the least of them to the greatest… for I will forgive their iniquity." That's why people with no church background can come to know God so deeply once they grasp they're forgiven. Declare it daily: "I am the righteousness of God in Christ." The more you do, the more you'll know Him.

messages.text: God made Christ "head over all things to the church." The church isn't as poor as a church mouse. It's the body of the One who reigns.
messages.explanation:
God raised Christ "far above all principality and power and might and dominion, and every name that is named… and put all things under His feet, and gave Him to be head over all things to the church, which is His body." Jesus is head over all things for your benefit. Whatever you're facing has a name, and you're seated in Him far above it.

The world calls the church a dull building for old people, "poor as a church mouse." But the church is the body of the One who said, "All authority has been given to Me in heaven and on earth." Things that loom over you are, in God's eyes, under your feet.

messages.text: Guilt can't be in two places. If Jesus bore it, you don't have to.
messages.explanation:
In prayer one day, these words came to Joseph Prince so clearly that he got up to write them down: "Jesus cannot bear guilt while you are bearing guilt. Guilt cannot be in two places. Either it's on Him, or it's on you. If it's on you and you bear it, it cannot be on Him. Where guilt is, there can be no restoration."

It sounds simple, but it changes everything. When you've failed, carrying the guilt yourself doesn't honour God. It treats the cross as if it wasn't enough. Look to Jesus and say, "Lord, You bore this guilt. I won't carry it." Then expect Him to restore.

messages.text: The guilt offering required restoring "its full value, add one-fifth more." Jesus became our guilt offering: 120% restoration.
messages.explanation:
Under the law, someone who had cheated, stolen or lied about another's property had to bring an asham, a guilt offering, and "restore its full value, add one-fifth more to it." It wasn't enough to repay; the wronged party received 120%. Isaiah says the Messiah's soul was made an asham, a guilt offering. And in a psalm Jesus quoted at the Last Supper: "Then I restored that which I did not take away."

Jesus took the place of the guilty one, so He's the one who restores, and you've been made the righteous one who receives. Where the enemy has robbed you, whether of health, peace or provision, don't wallow in guilt. Say, "Because of the cross, I receive 120% restoration here."

messages.text: "There is therefore now no condemnation": in Greek, ouden, none at all, no exceptions.
messages.explanation:
The word Paul uses is a strong negative that shuts the door completely. Not a little condemnation, not some: none. "For those who are in Christ Jesus." Notice: not Jesus Christ, the name often used of Him in His earthly ministry, but Christ Jesus, the risen, glorified Lord at the Father's right hand. That's who you're in.

Can the glorified Christ ever be condemned? Then neither can you. He died to sin once for all: to its condemnation and judgment. You're enveloped in Him, like someone in the depths of the ocean, surrounded on every side. And verse 2 follows verse 1: "The law of the Spirit of life in Christ Jesus has made me free from the law of sin and death."

messages.text: Jesus said, "Neither do I condemn you; go and sin no more." No condemnation comes first, and that's what empowers you.
messages.explanation:
The church often gets the order backwards: "Sort out your life first, then we won't condemn you." But Jesus spoke to a woman caught in the act of adultery only hours before. First, "Neither do I condemn you." Then, "Go and sin no more."

Receiving no condemnation while you're still in your mess is what gives you the power to walk free. Psychiatrists observe that guilt lies at the root of addictions: the more guilty you feel, the more you repeat what you're ashamed of. Grace breaks the cycle. When you know how completely you're loved and forgiven, the desire for sin itself begins to fade.

messages.text: "Look around you and be distressed. Look within you and be depressed. Look to Christ and be at rest."
messages.explanation:
That saying is often attributed to Corrie ten Boom, and it's exactly what the accuser exploits. In Hebrew, ha-satan means the prosecutor. A prosecutor never argues the defendant's good points. He'll remind you of every failure and tell you that even your good deeds weren't good enough. The more self-occupied you become, the deeper you sink.

The way out isn't trying harder to feel better about yourself. It's looking away from yourself to Jesus and His finished work. When the enemy accuses you, tell him, "Go and check Jesus. If you find anything wrong with His obedience, come back and talk to me."

messages.text: "I am the righteousness of God in Christ." A man in his 70s said it daily, and a 20-year addiction ended.
messages.explanation:
A brother from South Carolina wrote that he'd smoked pot for twenty years, from his fifties into his seventies, and had tried to quit many times. After hearing testimonies, he began declaring, "I am the righteousness of God in Christ." He said it felt ridiculous, but he did it in faith. Within weeks he was free, with no withdrawal and no desire to smoke again.

That's real transformation: not gritting your teeth against something you still crave, but being freed even from the wanting. Say it in the middle of your struggle, not after you've won. It isn't a lie. It's what God says is true of you.

messages.text: If a debtor's bill is paid but he doesn't know it, he still hides from his creditor. Believe the news.
messages.explanation:
Imagine owing someone $10,000 you can't repay. Every time you see him, the debt weighs on your conscience. Then someone pays it for you, and more: they give him a million. He's not out of pocket because of you; he's been enriched. But if you never hear about it, or don't believe the person who tells you, you'll still avoid him and feel the weight, though the debt is gone.

That's what Hebrews means by worshippers who, "once purified, would have had no more consciousness of sins." Through the cross, God has received far more glory than our sin ever robbed Him of. Believe the messenger, and "draw near with a true heart in full assurance of faith."

messages.text: The one with an argument can't take away the experience of the one who once was blind and now sees.
messages.explanation:
After Jesus healed a man born blind, the Pharisees interrogated him and insisted that Jesus was a sinner. His answer was simple: "Whether He is a sinner or not I do not know. One thing I know: that though I was blind, now I see." Nobody can reason away what happened to you.

That's why testimonies matter. "They overcame him by the blood of the Lamb and by the word of their testimony." Share what Jesus has done in your life; it's the gospel in a form no one can argue with. And when you're believing for your own breakthrough, read others' testimonies, perhaps while you wait for a doctor's appointment. What He did for them, He'll do for you.

messages.text: You are a spirit, you have a soul, you live in a body. God made you to be led by your spirit.
messages.explanation:
Your body has the five senses. Your soul holds your mind, emotions and will. Your spirit, the real you that's born again, has communion with God, intuition and conscience. Since the fall, people have been led either by their bodies ("I want it now") or by their minds ("If I don't understand it, stop it").

God doesn't want you to ignore your mind or neglect your body; He wants your spirit to lead. That's where you commune with Him, not by chasing feelings, which rise and fall. And that's where "the Spirit Himself bears witness with our spirit that we are children of God." When you're about to sign that deal and there's an unrest deep down you can't explain, pause and pray. Your intuition is quicker than your reasoning.

messages.text: "The just shall live by faith" can be read, "He who through faith is righteous shall live."
messages.explanation:
Paul says he isn't ashamed of the gospel, "for it is the power of God to salvation." The word soteria includes healing, wholeness, deliverance and well-being. And what is this gospel? "In it the righteousness of God is revealed from faith to faith." Not only forgiveness of sins, but righteousness as a gift.

We often read "the just shall live by faith" as "righteous people must trust God for their needs." But the Greek can also be read, as several translations render it, "he who through faith is righteous shall live." Those who are righteous by faith will live: life that swallows up sickness, depression and death.

messages.text: "The Spirit is life because of righteousness." Let that life flow from your spirit to your mind, and from your mind to your body.
messages.explanation:
"If Christ is in you, the body is dead because of sin, but the Spirit is life because of righteousness. But if the Spirit of Him who raised Jesus from the dead dwells in you, He… will also give life to your mortal bodies." Mortal bodies: this isn't the rapture, when we'll be transformed. It's life for your body now.

Your spirit is already alive and righteous. The question is whether that life reaches your soul and body. Your mind is the gate: "to be spiritually minded is life and peace." So keep your mind on who you are in Christ. When you begin to feel your righteousness, not just know it, you're one step from your body. Depression lifts, and healing flows.

messages.text: Isaiah saw a people who would say, "Surely in the Lord I have righteousness and strength."
messages.explanation:
"Surely one shall say, 'In the Lord I have righteousness and strength.' To Him men shall come, and all shall be ashamed who are incensed against Him. In the Lord all the descendants of Israel shall be justified, and shall glory." Paul draws on this same passage when he writes that every knee shall bow to Jesus.

Isaiah was looking ahead to you: a people who don't boast in their own goodness but say, "My righteousness and my strength are in the Lord." That isn't pride; it's a gift you didn't make yourself. And as you say it, those who rage against you will be ashamed.

messages.text: Paul preached that through Jesus you're not only forgiven, but "justified from all things" the law could never justify you from.
messages.explanation:
We actually have one of Paul's sermons recorded, preached in the synagogue at Pisidian Antioch. It reached its climax here: "Let it be known to you, brethren, that through this Man is preached to you the forgiveness of sins; and by Him everyone who believes is justified from all things from which you could not be justified by the law of Moses."

Forgiveness wipes the slate clean. Justification goes further: you're declared righteous. Much preaching stops at the first and calls it the gospel. But you're not just a pardoned sinner; you're a new creation, born righteous. Treasure that gift. It's the blessing of Abraham, who was justified by faith.

messages.text: "Lord, I can't break this relationship. You break it for me."
messages.explanation:
A woman who was born again wrote of being trapped for five years in an adulterous relationship. She knew it was wrong, broke it off again and again, and always went back. Guilt and condemnation took her peace. Then she began listening to teaching on God's forgiveness and declaring that she was the righteousness of God in Christ. She heard that God can be asked to end a relationship we can't end ourselves, so she prayed that very prayer.

It didn't happen overnight. But one day the relationship ended, and she was free, without the guilt. Sin doesn't have the final say. "Sin shall not have dominion over you, for you are not under law but under grace."

messages.text: "He made Him… to be sin… that we might become the righteousness of God." Two different Greek words for made.
messages.explanation:
The first "made," poieo, means to fashion, the way an artist crafts something; it's the root of poiema, "workmanship," from which we get poem. There was divine artistry in the way God laid all our sins on His Son. The second word, ginomai, means to come into being, something that never existed before, like a birth.

When you were born again, you were born righteous: a new creation "created in righteousness and true holiness," a living poem declaring His excellencies. You didn't make yourself; "we are His workmanship." So stop trying to improve yourself by your own efforts. Look to the One who creates beautifully.

messages.text: Leviticus calls the burnt offering "holy," but the sin offering "most holy." Even bearing our sin, Jesus was most holy.
messages.explanation:
The burnt offering pictures Christ offering Himself wholly to glorify the Father. But in the sin offering we see Him made sin for us, and our thoughts might drift into seeing Him as somehow tainted. So God labelled the sin offering "most holy," adding that whatever touched it became holy.

At the very moment He became sin with our sin, He was most holy in God's eyes. He "committed no sin, nor was deceit found in His mouth." And because we've touched Him by faith, we've been made holy too. Let that guard how you think of Him, and of yourself.

messages.text: Never judge your standing by your state. Judge your state by your standing.
messages.explanation:
Your state goes up and down: some days you're joyful, some days angry, depressed, tempted. Your standing never changes: in Christ, you are the righteousness of God. You weren't made righteous by your obedience, so your disobedience can't make you unrighteous. "By one Man's obedience many will be made righteous."

The devil wants to define you by your latest failure. Don't deny the sin or excuse it. Look it in the eye and say, "This isn't who I am. I'm not an angry person or a fearful person. I'm the righteousness of God in Christ." Who you are will overcome what you do.

messages.text: Of David's many sons, God chose Bathsheba's to be king. The mouth that denied Jesus preached at Pentecost.
messages.explanation:
"Where sin abounded, grace abounded much more." The word for sin abounding means increase, something you can count. Grace hyperperisseuo: overflowing, and then more piled on top. And grace abounds at the very location where sin increased.

David sinned grievously with Bathsheba. Yet from that same woman came Solomon, whom God chose above all David's other sons. Peter denied Jesus three times with oaths and curses; weeks later, that same mouth preached the first gospel sermon, and three thousand were saved. That's no licence to sin. It's hope: the place of your greatest failure can become the place of your greatest testimony.

messages.text: "Lord, I give You my whole life, including my stutter." He chose the very weakness to display His grace.
messages.explanation:
As a schoolboy, Joseph Prince stammered so badly he could barely string a sentence together. A teacher would make him stand and read aloud just to watch his ears turn red while classmates laughed. When he was saved, he felt almost sorry for the Lord: "You didn't get much. I don't think I can even share the gospel with a friend. But I give You my whole life, plus my stuttering."

He never imagined he'd preach. Yet the very area where he fell short became the place God's grace overflowed. "My strength is made perfect in weakness." Don't hide your weakness from God. Hand it to Him, and watch it become the platform for His glory.

messages.text: Paul was accused of saying "Let us sin that grace may abound." If no one accuses us of that, are we preaching his gospel?
messages.explanation:
"Shall we continue in sin that grace may abound? Certainly not! How shall we who died to sin live any longer in it?" Paul raised the question because people were already slandering him: "Let us do evil that good may come." Martyn Lloyd-Jones, the famous Westminster preacher, once observed that if our preaching never draws that accusation, perhaps we aren't preaching grace the way Paul did.

Notice Paul's answer. He doesn't say, "Try hard not to." He says it's impossible to live in sin, because you died to it. A true believer may stumble into sin, but can't make it a home. Grace that's truly understood doesn't produce licence. It produces people who have no desire to go back.

messages.text: Dying Rachel named her son Ben-Oni, "son of my sorrow." His father renamed him Benjamin, "son of my right hand."
messages.explanation:
When Rachel gave birth to Joseph, she named him in faith: "The Lord shall add to me another son." Years later, as she died giving birth to that second son, she called him Ben-Oni, son of my sorrow. "But his father called him Benjamin": son of my right hand, the place of power, favour and blessing.

It's a picture of a generation God is raising up in these last days, a grace generation. Some will try to load it with guilt: "Your mother died because of you; grace is ruining the church." But it's the Father who names this generation, not the critics. You're not a child of sorrow. You're a son or daughter of His right hand.

messages.text: Benjamin received five times as much food as his brothers, and five changes of clothing. Five is the number of grace.
messages.explanation:
When Joseph finally saw Benjamin, his only full brother, he had to leave the room to weep. His first words to him were, "God be gracious to you, my son." At the meal, "Benjamin's serving was five times as much as any of theirs." Later Joseph gave each brother a change of clothes, "but to Benjamin he gave three hundred pieces of silver and five changes of garments."

Jesus said not to worry about what you'll eat or wear, and here is a generation lavishly supplied with both. Five recurs throughout Scripture as a number of grace. Five changes of garments may also picture a manifold grace: an anointing that can flow in more than one way. Grace doesn't ration.

messages.text: Zechariah couldn't speak until he wrote, "His name is John": Yohanan, "the Lord is gracious."
messages.explanation:
When Gabriel announced that Zechariah's elderly wife would bear a son named John, the old priest didn't believe it, and he was struck mute until the promise was fulfilled. Nine months later, relatives wanted to name the baby after his father. Zechariah asked for a tablet and wrote, "His name is John." Immediately his mouth was opened, and he began to praise God and prophesy.

John, Yohanan, means "the Lord is gracious." Those who don't believe the message of grace often find they have nothing to say; the passion to share dries up. But the moment you write "grace" over your life, your mouth is loosed again.

messages.text: At the well, she called Him "a Jew," then "Sir," then "a prophet," then "the Christ," and then she became an evangelist.
messages.explanation:
Nicodemus, a learned teacher of Israel, came slowly to faith; only after the cross did he openly honour Jesus. But the Samaritan woman, living with a man who wasn't her husband after five marriages, grew in revelation within hours. "How is it that You, being a Jew…?" "Sir, You have nothing to draw with." "Sir, I perceive that You are a prophet." Then Jesus said, "I who speak to you am He."

She left her waterpot and ran into the town: "Come, see a Man who told me all things that I ever did. Could this be the Christ?" Many believed because of her. It was to her, not the theologian, that Jesus revealed true worship. Grace can transform people faster than anyone imagines.

messages.text: At the cross, John was the one disciple still there. He called himself "the disciple whom Jesus loved."
messages.explanation:
When Jesus hung on the cross and needed someone to care for His mother, all the other disciples had fled. John was there. "Woman, behold your son!… Behold your mother!" Yet John never called himself "the disciple who loved Jesus." He was conscious of Jesus' love for him, not his love for Jesus.

That's the secret. Those most conscious of receiving His love end up serving Him most, often without realising they're serving at all. You don't come to Jesus mainly to learn how to serve Him harder. You come to learn how to receive, and out of that, service flows.

messages.text: As Joseph sent his brothers home, he said, "See that you do not quarrel along the way."
messages.explanation:
Joseph had just revealed himself, forgiven them and loaded them with provisions. Then, as they set out, he added a very human word of advice. He knew what would happen otherwise: "It was your idea to sell him!" "No, it was yours!" "I wasn't even there!"

It's a word for us too, as we journey home toward the One who forgave us. Don't fight about whose fault the past was. Don't turn on each other along the way. Think about His glory, carry His provision, and love one another as He has loved you.

messages.text: "He who was born according to the flesh persecuted him who was born according to the Spirit." Law persecutes grace, never the reverse.
messages.explanation:
Paul says Hagar and Sarah represent two covenants: Hagar is Mount Sinai, "which gives birth to bondage," and Sarah is the Jerusalem above, which is free. Both sons had the same father, Abraham. "But, as he who was born according to the flesh then persecuted him who was born according to the Spirit, even so it is now."

It's always the son of the law who persecutes the son of grace. Many who criticise grace have the same heavenly Father as you, but not the same mother. And notice Paul's conclusion: "Cast out the bondwoman and her son." Sarah doesn't need Hagar's help to raise Isaac. Grace doesn't need the law brought back to keep you holy.

messages.text: A bullock, a lamb or a pair of doves: God accepted every size of burnt offering. Your capacity to see Jesus is what grows.
messages.explanation:
Leviticus 1 describes three burnt offerings: a bull from the herd for those who could afford it, a sheep or goat, and for the poorest, turtledoves or pigeons. Each one rose as "a sweet aroma to the Lord," because each pictured His Son. God never said, "Come back when you can bring a bull." A woman who only touched the hem of His garment received all the healing she needed.

Yet the sizes speak of capacity. Only for the bull does Scripture mention laying hands on its head, and skinning it and cutting it in pieces. A bigger revelation of Jesus enlarges what you can receive. "Grace and peace be multiplied to you in the knowledge of God and of Jesus our Lord." Whatever size your offering today, keep growing in your view of Him.

messages.text: In Hebrew, Leviticus is called Vayikra, "And He called." The word for offering, korban, means to draw near.
messages.explanation:
Leviticus is the book many believers skip, yet it opens with God calling, not demanding. "Now the Lord called to Moses… 'When any one of you brings an offering to the Lord…'" The Hebrew for offering, korban, comes from a root meaning to come near. Every sacrifice in the book was God's way of bringing people close.

All those offerings point to the one sacrifice of Jesus. Because of Him you don't stand at a distance hoping you're good enough. "Having boldness to enter the Holiest by the blood of Jesus… let us draw near with a true heart in full assurance of faith." The offering has been made. You're called near.

messages.text: The worshipper laid his hand on the bullock's head: his sin went onto it, and its perfection came onto him.
messages.explanation:
"He shall put his hand on the head of the burnt offering, and it will be accepted on his behalf." The word for accepted, ratzah, carries the idea of delight and pleasure. Laying on hands was identification. The spotless animal took the offerer's place and died as if it were guilty, while the offerer was received with all its unblemished acceptance.

That's what happened when you put your faith in Jesus. Your sins went to Him; His righteousness came to you. So stop identifying with what you were: lost, condemned, under the curse. Identify with Him. You're accepted in the Beloved, and God takes delight in you.

messages.text: To create the world, God only had to speak. To forgive you, He had to bleed.
messages.explanation:
When the prodigal came home, his father said, "Bring the fatted calf here and kill it." Animals were usually slaughtered out of sight, behind the house. But this father wanted it done in front of his son, so that he would see what his forgiveness had cost.

The calf wasn't fattened for work in the fields; it was raised for this one day of sacrifice. Jesus came for the same purpose. Your forgiveness is free to you, but it wasn't cheap. And because the price was so great, you never have to wonder whether it was enough.

messages.text: "A sweet aroma to the Lord" is literally an aroma of rest. Every time you draw near, God smells His Son on you.
messages.explanation:
The Hebrew phrase is reach nichoach, an aroma of rest, from the same root as Noah's name. When Noah stepped off the ark and offered burnt offerings, "the Lord smelled a soothing aroma," and He promised never again to curse the ground. God finds His rest in the sacrifice of His Son.

And now "we are to God the fragrance of Christ." When old Isaac blessed Jacob, he said, "The smell of my son is like the smell of a field which the Lord has blessed." Isaac was fooled; God isn't. He sees what Jesus did, and every time you pray, you come wrapped in that fragrance. Picture that, and you'll find yourself coming to Him at every turn.

messages.text: The Hebrew for peace offering is plural, shelamim: peace for spirit, soul and body. And shalom shares its root with paying in full.
messages.explanation:
Shalom already means completeness: health, wholeness, well-being. Leviticus puts it in the plural, peace in all its fullness. The same root gives the Hebrew verb for paying, making whole what was owed. Your peace was paid for, and it cost God His Son: "The chastisement for our peace was upon Him."

Notice too that the fat of the peace offering, the choicest part, was burned on top of the burnt offering already on the altar. Peace rests on the foundation of the burnt offering, our acceptance and righteousness in Christ. Know you're righteous in Him, and wholeness has something to stand on.

messages.text: The Lord restored Job's losses, twice as much, when he prayed for the friends who had wronged him.
messages.explanation:
Job's friends had added to his suffering with wrong words about God. God told them to bring burnt offerings, "and My servant Job shall pray for you." Job took a priest's place for the very people who had hurt him. "And the Lord restored Job's losses when he prayed for his friends. Indeed the Lord gave Job twice as much as he had before."

Under the law, the priest who offered someone's burnt offering kept its skin for himself. When you see those who've spoken against you as the righteousness of God in Christ and bless them, you share in the benefits of that offering. Try it: "Father, thank You that they're righteous in Christ. Give them wisdom and revelation. I bless them."

messages.text: "My people will dwell in a peaceful habitation, in secure dwellings, and in quiet resting places."
messages.explanation:
Isaiah continues, "though hail comes down on the forest, and the city is brought low in humiliation." The storms are real. Forests fall and cities are laid low. But God makes a distinction: "My people" dwell in peace and security in the middle of it.

Don't expect what the world expects. "The path of the just is like the shining sun, that shines ever brighter unto the perfect day." Ever brighter, not dimmer. Your days ahead are days of hope, not because the world is getting easier, but because you're His, and He has given you quietness and security forever.

messages.text: Drinking a glass of water puts the water in you. Jumping into a pool puts you in the water. That's the baptism in the Spirit.
messages.explanation:
On the evening He rose, Jesus breathed on His disciples and said, "Receive the Holy Spirit." They were born again; the Spirit now lived in them. Yet weeks later He told the same disciples to wait in Jerusalem for "the Promise of the Father… you shall be baptized with the Holy Spirit not many days from now… you shall receive power."

Every believer has the Spirit within; you can't be born again without Him. But baptizo means to immerse. It's one thing for Him to be in you, and another for you to be immersed in Him, clothed with power to be His witness. That's not only something you do; it's something you become. If you've never received this gift, simply ask.

messages.text: "They were all filled with the Holy Spirit and began to speak." The Spirit gives the words, but you do the speaking.
messages.explanation:
Many people wait for the Holy Spirit to take over their mouths. But read carefully: "They began to speak with other tongues, as the Spirit gave them utterance." The Spirit supplies the utterance; you voice it. He never possesses you or forces you; you can start and you can stop.

It's like the priests at the Jordan. The river didn't part until their feet touched the water. So after you've asked the Father for the Spirit, relax and begin to speak by faith. A trickle becomes a stream, and the stream becomes the "rivers of living water" Jesus promised.

messages.text: "I thank my God I speak with tongues more than you all; yet in the church…" People quote the second half and skip the first.
messages.explanation:
Paul told the Corinthians that in a church gathering he'd rather speak five words with understanding than ten thousand in a tongue, because no one can be taught by words they can't follow. But he began by saying he prayed in tongues more than all of them, and the Corinthians were hardly shy about it.

In private, praying in the Spirit edifies you and speaks mysteries to God. "I will pray with the spirit, and I will also pray with the understanding." Do both. Often after a season of praying in tongues, Scripture opens up, your English prayers go straight to the heart of the matter, and the five words you speak carry power.

messages.text: When you don't know what's troubling your child, pray in the Spirit. He knows exactly.
messages.explanation:
You can see something's wrong with your teenager but can't put your finger on it. Your mind might pray around the edges. The Holy Spirit knows exactly what's happening: perhaps a loneliness that's settled on them even among friends. When you pray in tongues, He prays through you what you can't articulate.

Keep going until you sense a release. Often your prayers in English then begin to flow, and you find yourself praying for the very thing the Spirit has already been praying. And the promise for your children is that they "shall be taught by the Lord": by Him, not just about Him. "And great shall be the peace of your children."

messages.text: "Be filled with the Spirit" is present tense: keep on being filled. The way? "Speaking… singing and making melody."
messages.explanation:
Paul contrasts being drunk with wine with being filled with the Spirit. The command is continuous and passive: let yourself be filled, again and again. And your active part is in the next verse: "speaking to one another in psalms and hymns and spiritual songs, singing and making melody in your heart to the Lord." When you're down or under attack, start singing, start praying in the Spirit.

Notice what follows straight after: wives, husbands, children, parents. Ephesians teaches more on family life than any other letter of Paul, and it puts this constant filling right before it. Your marriage and your parenting need more than techniques; they need the Spirit flowing through you.

messages.text: "Stir up the gift of God which is in you": fan it into flame. "For God has not given us a spirit of fear."
messages.explanation:
The word for gift here isn't the one used for the Holy Spirit Himself; it's charisma, the word for the spiritual gifts. And "stir up" means to fan into flame, like fanning embers until the fire catches. The next verse is joined to it: "For God has not given us a spirit of fear, but of power and of love and of a sound mind."

Most gifts of the Spirit operate as He wills. Praying in tongues is the one you can start whenever you choose. On a Hanukkah menorah, the central servant candle lights all the others. Praying in the Spirit is like that: as you fan it into flame, fear leaves and power, love and a sound mind flow.

messages.text: Know your wealth before your walk. You're seated with Christ; step down into your family like someone from heaven.
messages.explanation:
Ephesians opens with your riches: chosen, forgiven "according to the riches of His grace," raised up and seated with Christ in heavenly places. Only then does it talk about how you walk, and how you treat your spouse and children. The world teaches marriage and parenting by technique. God starts by telling you who you are.

Imagine an angel living with your family for a month: there'd be a dignity about him, without any holier-than-thou attitude. Jesus, "knowing that the Father had given all things into His hands, and that He had come from God and was going to God," rose and washed His disciples' feet. When you know what you have, humble service carries glory.

messages.text: Others ran, out of breath, with heavy bags. I stood at rest on the travelator, bags at my feet, and moved faster than all of them.
messages.explanation:
Joseph Prince received the theme for 2022 in a dream. He was in an airport on a moving walkway. All around him people were rushing, anxious, sprinting with heavy luggage. He had bags too, and they were heavy, but they rested on the travelator beside him. He was calm, and yet he was accelerating.

Rest and acceleration sound like opposites. In God's ways they belong together. "Come to Me… and I will give you rest" can be read, "I Myself will rest you." Your burdens don't disappear, but you don't have to carry them in your own strength. Enter His rest, and things that would have taken years can come to pass quickly.

messages.text: "The plowman shall overtake the reaper." Sowing and harvest so close together, they run into each other.
messages.explanation:
In Israel, wheat fields are ploughed in autumn and harvested months later in spring. The ploughman and the reaper never meet. But God says that when He rebuilds "the tabernacle of David, which has fallen down," the harvest will still be coming in when it's time to plough again, and "the treader of grapes [shall overtake] him who sows seed. The mountains shall drop sweet wine."

At the Jerusalem council, James quoted this very passage to explain the Gentiles coming to faith. God has been rebuilding David's tabernacle, His church, ever since. Expect acceleration: prayers answered, loved ones saved, healings springing forth speedily, and so much new wine that the tears of past years are swallowed up in joy.

messages.text: "Among the sons of my father, He was pleased with me." It's one thing to be loved by God. It's another to be liked by Him.
messages.explanation:
David told Israel's leaders that God chose Judah, then his father's house, "and among the sons of my father, He was pleased with me to make me king." God called him "a man after My own heart." God loves all His children, but He was fond of David.

Why? Others in Scripture were quick to repent. What set David apart was a longing from boyhood to bring the ark, the place of God's presence, to the centre of Israel's life. The ark pictured Jesus. Whatever you do with God's beloved Son, God does with you. Honour Him, make Him central, and you'll find God delights in you.

messages.text: The law was kept inside the ark, under the mercy seat. When men of Beth Shemesh lifted the lid to look in, they died.
messages.explanation:
Inside the ark were three things that recalled Israel's rebellion: the pot of manna they despised, Aaron's rod that budded to end their murmuring, and the tablets of the law they broke. God covered them all with the mercy seat, where the blood was sprinkled. Paul says God set forth Jesus as a "propitiation," hilasterion, the same word the Greek Old Testament uses for the mercy seat.

When the Philistines returned the ark, men of Beth Shemesh lifted the lid to look inside, and judgment fell. Many believers do the same today, pulling the law back out from under the blood. Leave it covered. Mercy sits above the law.

messages.text: Uzzah, whose name means strength, reached out to steady the ark. God's glory doesn't need man's hand to hold it up.
messages.explanation:
David put the ark on a new cart, the way the Philistines had, instead of on the shoulders of the Levites as God had commanded. When the oxen stumbled, Uzzah stretched out his hand, and he died. David named the place Perez-uzzah: perez means breach. It was the first breach in David's story.

The Levites had carried the ark on their shoulders through forty years in the wilderness, and no one had died. God's way brings life; man's inventions bring breaches. The problem at Perez wasn't sin. It was human strength intruding on God's work. Lay down your own effort and let Him carry what's His.
