When God sent Haggai, he didn't discuss the king's decree. He said, "This people says, 'The time has not come that the Lord's house should be built.' Is it time for you yourselves to dwell in your panelled houses?" Circumstances can become an excuse. Put first what God puts first.

messages.text: One bird asked another, "Why are humans so anxious?" "Maybe they don't have a heavenly Father like we do."
messages.explanation:
"Look at the birds of the air, for they neither sow nor reap nor gather into barns; yet your heavenly Father feeds them. Are you not of more value than they?" Birds don't phone ahead to book a table. They don't know there's a recession. They sing.

Jesus begins that passage with "therefore," right after saying, "You cannot serve God and mammon." Much of our anxiety comes from chasing money as if it were our provider. Life is more than food, and your body more than clothes. Your Father knows what you need; you're worth far more to Him than a sparrow.

messages.text: You'll trust a pilot you've never met with your life at 30,000 feet. Why demand that God prove Himself first?
messages.explanation:
The captain's voice comes over the speaker, calm and pleasant, and you settle back and take off your shoes. You've never seen him, and you don't know what kind of night he had. Yet when it comes to God, we say, "Show me a sign first." People who've never studied how air conditioning works still switch it on.

Your head will never be satisfied; reason always wants to sit on the throne. Let your spirit lead, and your mind follow. And if you ever wonder, "What if it isn't true?", remember: trusting Jesus has filled your life with joy, peace and freedom. If He's real and you reject Him, you lose everything.

messages.text: Never tell your child, "You're a liar." Say, "You're a forgiven child of God who told a lie, and that's not who we are."
messages.explanation:
Children who are never corrected often grow up resenting their parents; correction tells them they're loved enough to have boundaries. But how you correct matters. Labelling a child by their failure reinforces it.

Correct them the gospel way: show them what sin did, then show them Jesus, who loves them and has borne it. Remind them of their identity: "We're Jesus people, and Jesus people don't lie." Let them experience forgiveness, so that who they are can overcome what they did. That's how your heavenly Father corrects you too.

messages.text: Before you envy someone's harvest, ask what they've sown. Nobody sees the seed going into the ground.
messages.explanation:
Stand at the edge of a field while a farmer scatters seed, and from a distance you can't see a thing. Come back months later and everyone sees the harvest. It's easy to look at someone's blessing and assume it just fell on them, without knowing what they gave, served or sacrificed in the hidden years.

It works the other way too. Some of us are living off past harvests and have stopped sowing. Keep sowing into God's house and His purposes, even when no one notices. "Let us not grow weary while doing good, for in due season we shall reap if we do not lose heart."

messages.text: "The anointing which you have received from Him abides in you." It doesn't leave when you stumble.
messages.explanation:
As a teenager, Joseph Prince dabbled in the occult and New Age teachings sprinkled with Bible verses. Ouija boards don't contact the dead; they open the door to familiar spirits impersonating them, and he suffered terrible nightmares. One day, during a Bible study on returning to your first love, something deep inside told him, "What you've been reading isn't right."

John wrote about those trying to deceive believers: "The anointing… abides in you, and you do not need that anyone teach you; but as the same anointing teaches you concerning all things." When a teaching or a news report feels slanted, listen to that inner witness. It doesn't come and go with your behaviour; it abides.

messages.text: "I will give you rest" and "you will find rest for your souls" are two different rests. One is given; the other is found by learning from Him.
messages.explanation:
"Come to Me… and I will give you rest": that's the rest of a cleansed conscience, received the moment you know all your sins are forgiven. Many believers have it, yet their souls are still restless: anxious, competitive, easily provoked.

The second rest comes as you "take My yoke upon you and learn from Me, for I am gentle and lowly in heart." Notice the centre of the passage: learn from Me. You don't find rest for your soul by trying harder to be calm. You find it by beholding Jesus, until His gentleness becomes yours.

messages.text: Meekness isn't weakness. It's strength under control.
messages.explanation:
Jesus called Himself gentle and lowly, yet He made a whip of cords and single-handedly drove the money-changers out of the temple. When soldiers came to arrest Him, they fell backwards at His word. He said, "Follow Me," and rugged fishermen left their nets.

What the world calls power, losing your temper, cursing, forcing your way, isn't strength at all; it's being out of control. Road rage, the race to the front of the queue, the need to win every argument, often come from insecurity. Someone secure in the Father's love can afford to let others go first.

messages.text: "Turn the other cheek" isn't about being a doormat. It's about refusing to let the other person set the terms.
messages.explanation:
Jesus said, "Whoever slaps you on your right cheek, turn the other to him also." Most people are right-handed, so a blow to the right cheek is a backhanded slap: an insult, a challenge to fight. Jesus wasn't telling you to be weak. He was telling you not to react on your opponent's terms.

Don't let people push your buttons, and don't become a garbage truck for someone else's bitterness and gossip. Respond out of the Spirit instead of reacting out of the flesh. When you take back the initiative, you're no longer controlled by other people's moods.

messages.text: "I will say of the Lord, 'He is my refuge.'" Trusting God isn't silent. It speaks.
messages.explanation:
"I will say of the Lord, 'He is my refuge and my fortress; my God, in Him I will trust.'" The verse begins with saying and ends with trusting, and they belong together. "We also believe and therefore speak." God looked at the darkness and didn't describe it; He said, "Let there be light."

It's easy to say "I trust God" while talking all day about how bad things are. What are you saying about the Lord in your situation? "He is my refuge. He turns the water of my marriage into wine. He gives me success." Say it every day; that's what trust sounds like.

messages.text: "As long as he sought the Lord, God made him prosper." Seek Yahweh, your covenant friend, and Elohim moves everything else.
messages.explanation:
In the King James, "LORD" in capitals renders Yahweh, God's covenant name; "God" is Elohim, the Creator who rules all things. Of King Uzziah it's written, "As long as he sought the LORD, God made him prosper." Surrounded by enemy chariots, Jehoshaphat "cried out, and the LORD helped him, and God diverted them from him."

David told Goliath, "I come to you in the name of the LORD of hosts… that all the earth may know that there is a God in Israel." The world can only know Him as Elohim. You can know Him as your covenant friend. Don't just seek His hand; seek His face, and He'll move circumstances for you.

messages.text: Even as cities rejected Him, Jesus said, "I thank You, Father." Praise didn't depend on approval.
messages.explanation:
Jesus had done many miracles in Capernaum, yet it didn't repent; He warned it would fare worse than Sodom. "At that time Jesus answered and said, 'I thank You, Father, Lord of heaven and earth, that You have hidden these things from the wise and prudent and have revealed them to babes.'" And it's in that same moment of rejection that He says, "Come to Me… I will give you rest."

No one could flatter Jesus into a good opinion of them, and no one could insult Him into a bitter one. He moved by the Spirit, not by people's reactions. Being yoked with Him means His peace becomes yours, even when you're misunderstood.

messages.text: Don't look to your spouse for what only Jesus can give. No one can fill that place but Him.
messages.explanation:
God ordained marriage, and it's a gift. But a spouse can't be your god. When two people each look to the other to satisfy their deepest longings, both feel disappointed, and the hurt comes out in harsh words. Get a new spouse, and the same problem follows, because you're still the same.

Jesus told the woman at the well, who'd had five husbands, "Whoever drinks of the water that I shall give him will never thirst." Draw your deepest fulfilment from Him. Then you can love your spouse freely, as someone already full, rather than demanding from them what only He can supply.

messages.text: "Grace and truth came through Jesus Christ." In Hebrew thought that's chesed ve'emet, and every time it shows up, something good happens.
messages.explanation:
Some say grace is God's soft side and truth His hard side, so we must balance them. But in the Greek, "grace and truth came" takes a singular verb: one reality, like buttered bread. A Jewish writer like John would have thought of chesed ve'emet, a phrase the Old Testament uses again and again.

Abraham's servant found Rebekah and said, "Blessed be the Lord… who has not forsaken His mercy and His truth." Jacob, coming home a wealthy man, prayed, "I am not worthy of the least of all the mercies and of all the truth… for I crossed over this Jordan with my staff, and now I have become two companies." Grace and truth always brings provision, guidance and blessing.

messages.text: "God is able to make all grace abound toward you… always having all sufficiency in all things." A cup has to be full before it can overflow.
messages.explanation:
Read it slowly: all grace; abounding toward you; always, in good times and bad; all sufficiency; in all things. And the purpose: "that you… may have an abundance for every good work."

This isn't about loving money; "the love of money is a root of all kinds of evil," whether you have much or little. It's about being so supplied that you can bless others. The poor can't lift the poor. God fills your cup so it can run over into your family, your church and your nation. Walk out today conscious that grace is abounding toward you.

messages.text: "Of His fullness we have all received, and grace for grace": as one wave of grace is spent, the next one is already arriving.
messages.explanation:
The word "for" can mean in place of. As soon as one grace has been used up, another takes its place, like waves rolling onto a beach, one after another, without end. His fullness never runs low.

That's why you don't need to feel ready now for what's ahead. "I couldn't cope with children." "I'm not ready for marriage." "I could never handle that loss." When you reach that stage of life, the grace for it will be there. Many look back and say, "I wish I'd known; the grace was there all along."

messages.text: A servant forgiven millions choked a man who owed him little. Bitterness hands you over to the tormentors.
messages.explanation:
The king forgave a debt no one could ever repay, purely out of compassion. The servant walked out and seized a fellow servant over a small debt and threw him into prison. The king said, "Should you not also have had compassion on your fellow servant, just as I had pity on you?" and delivered him to the torturers. "So My heavenly Father also will do to you if each of you, from his heart, does not forgive."

God doesn't send sickness, but bitterness opens doors to things that torment. Joseph Prince says that since his teens he's made a habit of forgiving quickly, even an irritation on the road: "Father, I forgive that person." Holding bitterness is like drinking poison and expecting the other person to suffer. You've been forgiven so much.

messages.text: Four lepers said, "Why are we sitting here until we die?" One step, and God routed the whole army.
messages.explanation:
Samaria was besieged and starving. Outside the gate, four lepers reasoned that they would die if they stayed, so they might as well go to the Syrian camp and hope for mercy. As they walked, the Lord made the Syrians hear the sound of a great army, and they fled, leaving everything behind.

The lepers ate and drank and gathered silver and gold. Then they said, "We are not doing right. This day is a day of good news, and we remain silent." We have good news a starving world needs. Husbands, wives and whole families are being transformed by it. Don't keep it to yourself.

messages.text: When Noah was found drunk and uncovered, two sons walked in backwards and covered him.
messages.explanation:
Ham saw his father's nakedness and went to tell his brothers. Shem and Japheth took a garment, walked backwards so as not to look, and covered him. When someone in a place of honour falls, our part isn't to spread the story but to cover and let God deal with it.

It's a sad sight when believers post videos tearing down other ministers over secondary issues while the world watches. Unity isn't built on agreeing on every peripheral doctrine; it's built around Christ. "By this all will know that you are My disciples, if you have love for one another." Don't give those attacks your views.

messages.text: In Jericho, the city under Joshua's curse, a blind beggar cried, "Son of David, have mercy on me!" The Son of God stood still.
messages.explanation:
Joshua cursed anyone who would rebuild Jericho. Bartimaeus means son of Timaeus; he isn't even given a name of his own, just a blind beggar by the road. Once, at Joshua's word, the sun stood still. Now the Son of God, who made the sun, stood still for a nameless beggar crying for grace.

He threw aside his beggar's cloak, the badge of his old life, and came to Jesus. His eyes were opened. Jesus said, "Go your way," and he "followed Jesus on the road." From then on, Jesus' way was his way. Wherever grace and truth arrives, curses break and lives are made new.

messages.text: The Sea of Galilee teems with fish; the Dead Sea holds nothing alive. One gives out; the other only takes in.
messages.explanation:
Both are fed by the Jordan. The Sea of Galilee lets water flow out again, and it has been full of fish since the days Peter's nets broke. The Dead Sea, the lowest place on earth, has no outlet. It only receives, and nothing lives in it.

God isn't against you having more than enough; He "gives us richly all things to enjoy." But He commands the rich "to do good, that they be rich in good works, ready to give." Be a channel, not a reservoir. If God can get it through you, He'll get it to you.

messages.text: "The land… is an exceedingly good land": in Hebrew, very, very good. God compares His land with His Book.
messages.explanation:
"A land of brooks of water, of fountains and springs that flow out of valleys and hills; a land of wheat and barley, of vines and fig trees and pomegranates… a land in which you will eat bread without scarcity, in which you will lack nothing." Joshua and Caleb called it me'od me'od, very, very good.

The Bible is like that land: bread to strengthen you, wine to gladden, figs and honey for sweetness, olive oil for anointing. And notice where the springs break out: in the valleys as well as on the hills. When you're going through a valley, open the Book. There are fountains there for you.

messages.text: Caleb promised his daughter to whoever took Kiriath Sepher, "city of the book." Othniel, "lion of God," took it.
messages.explanation:
The town had once been called Debir, which can suggest an oracle or word, and later Kiriath Sepher, "city of the book." Othniel conquered it and received Achsah, whose name means anklet, a picture of possessing every place your foot treads. It's the Lion of the tribe of Judah who "has prevailed to open the scroll."

Achsah then asked her father, "Give me a blessing… give me also springs of water," and he gave her the upper springs and the lower springs. Don't be shy about asking God for more. Dig into His Word, and He'll give you power to possess what you find there.

messages.text: "A man's wisdom makes his face shine, and the sternness of his face is changed."
messages.explanation:
You can often tell who has been spending time in the Word. There's a light in their faces, a lifting of the hardness. God's wisdom changes you from the inside, and it shows on the outside.

God even commanded Israel's kings to keep a copy of the law and "read it all the days of his life… that he may prolong his days." Picture an old saint in a rocking chair with an open Bible; perhaps that's part of why they're still here. "Hear, my son, and receive my sayings, and the years of your life will be many."

messages.text: Diagnosed with a tumour, a businessman asked his wife for a Bible. Peace came first, then joy, then healing.
messages.explanation:
Norman Vincent Peale told of meeting a business leader who wasn't a churchgoer. When doctors found a growth on his jaw, he went home discouraged and, unexpectedly, asked his wife to bring him a Bible. He didn't know where to start, so he simply began reading. A deep peace came over him. As he kept reading, longer each day, an inner joy followed. Some time later the doctors found he was free of it, and he remained well more than twenty years on.

God's words "are life to those who find them, and health to all their flesh." Don't worry about where to begin. Put a Bible where you'll see it, and just start reading.

messages.text: Muse means to ponder. Amusement can mean not pondering. Switch off now and then, and meditate.
messages.explanation:
Many believers are strong at the gym but spiritually anaemic: fed on streaming shows and endless scrolling, starved of the Word. It's hard to meditate on Scripture on a phone that pings with messages. Amusement isn't wrong, but it was never meant to crowd out meditation.

"This Book of the Law shall not depart from your mouth, but you shall meditate in it day and night… then you will have good success." Good success doesn't cost you your family, your church or your time with God. If it does, it isn't good success. Make room to sit with the Book and let it speak.

messages.text: "Sanctify them by Your truth. Your word is truth." Holy really means uncommon.
messages.explanation:
Holiness isn't about drab clothes or a list of rules. The opposite of holy is common. To be sanctified is to be set apart: steady when marriages around you are falling apart, at peace while others are anxious, healthy when sickness is common.

God surrounded ancient Israel with natural protection: sea to the west, deserts to the south and east, mountains to the north. Yet He placed it as a land bridge between Africa, Europe and Asia, so the nations would pass through and learn His ways. In the same way, Jesus didn't pray for you to be taken out of the world, but kept from evil. In a world full of slanted stories, His Word sets you apart and keeps you.

messages.text: Maybe you're not really depressed or angry. Maybe you're hungry.
messages.explanation:
A hungry husband can be a very short-tempered husband; the anger isn't the real problem. Many of us feel restless and empty, so we open the fridge, scroll a little longer, watch one more episode, and still feel hungry. "Why do you spend money for what is not bread, and your wages for what does not satisfy?"

Jeremiah shows the first thing to do with God's Word: "Your words were found, and I ate them, and Your word was to me the joy and rejoicing of my heart." Not "What must I do?" but eat. Feed on it until joy springs up. The enemy always goes after God's people's harvest; don't let anything steal your time in the Word.

messages.text: "Dad, the water runs right through the basket." "Yes, son, but look how clean the basket is now."
messages.explanation:
A farmer's boy complained that he didn't understand the Bible when he read it. His father handed him an old basket and sent him to the stream for water. Again and again it all drained out before he got back. The father pointed out that even though the basket couldn't hold the water, it had been washed clean.

You don't analyse the vitamins in every meal before you enjoy it. Read the Bible the same way. Even what you don't yet understand is cleansing you: "the washing of water by the word." Keep reading; understanding will come, and the washing happens all along.

messages.text: "You shall not muzzle an ox while it treads out the grain." Paul asks, "Is it oxen God is concerned about? Or… altogether for our sakes?"
messages.explanation:
Reading this law, you might simply see God's kindness to animals. Paul saw more: God was speaking about people, so that "he who ploughs should plough in hope." He applied it to those who sow spiritual things into others, that they shouldn't be shortchanged.

That's a key to reading the Old Testament. Don't turn it into a list of rules; look for God's love, and for what it shows you of Jesus. A God who wouldn't let a working ox go hungry isn't a tyrant. He makes sure those who labour for Him are fed.

messages.text: "He overthrew Pharaoh and his army in the Red Sea, for His mercy endures forever." Every judgment holds mercy for someone.
messages.explanation:
All twenty-six verses of Psalm 136 end with the same refrain: ki le'olam chasdo, for His lovingkindness endures forever. It's easy to say about creation and about dividing the Red Sea. But the psalmist says it even about Pharaoh's army drowning.

Pharaoh hardened his heart again and again despite repeated chances to relent. His army was charging toward Israel's families to destroy them. If someone were about to harm your child and God stopped them, you'd say, "His mercy endures forever." When you read of judgment in Scripture, look for whose side the mercy is on, and stand there.

messages.text: "Whoever takes the son gets everything."
messages.explanation:
A wealthy art collector's only son died in a war, and when the father died his priceless collection was auctioned. The first lot was a modest portrait of the son. No one bid, until the family's old servant, who had loved the boy, bought it for a few dollars. Then the auctioneer closed the sale: the will said that whoever took the son received the entire collection.

The Bible is God's photo album of His beloved Son. If you look away while He shows it, the album closes. But receive the Son, and you receive everything with Him. "He who has the Son has life," and you're a joint heir with Christ.

messages.text: Moses veiled his face because the glory was fading. "When one turns to the Lord, the veil is taken away."
messages.explanation:
Paul calls the law engraved on stone "the ministry of death" and "the ministry of condemnation." Even it had glory, but a fading glory, and Moses covered his face so Israel wouldn't see it fade. "The letter kills, but the Spirit gives life" is about law versus grace, not dull Bible study versus lively Bible study.

To this day a veil remains over many "when Moses is read." Turn to the Lord before you open your Bible, and the veil lifts. "We all, with unveiled face, beholding as in a mirror the glory of the Lord, are being transformed into the same image." One reader stamped "PAID" on every page of Leviticus, to remember he reads it in the light of the finished work.

messages.text: Jesus answered the Sadducees from one word: God said "I am," not "I was," the God of Abraham.
messages.explanation:
The Sadducees denied the resurrection. Jesus quoted God at the burning bush, "I am the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob," and concluded, "God is not the God of the dead, but of the living." The argument rests on the tense. Paul likewise argued from the word "Seed" being singular, pointing to Christ.

Every word of Scripture is God-breathed. In a world of edited videos and slanted stories, you're holding truth. And it's not only for pastors: Timothy knew the Scriptures from childhood, taught by his mother and grandmother, and they "are able to make you wise for salvation": healing, deliverance and wholeness included.

messages.text: "Through the comfort of the Scriptures we might have hope": not "I hope so," but a confident, joyful expectation of good.
messages.explanation:
The Greek elpis isn't wishful thinking. It's the confident expectation that good is coming. Without it, you wake up weary and dread the day; you lie awake imagining what might go wrong with your health, your children or your job. That's the absence of hope, and it often shows up as depression.

Where do you find hope? "Whatever things were written before were written for our learning." With talk of recession and shortages, read how God's people fared in famine. Abraham's blessing didn't exempt him from famine, but Isaac sowed in a famine year "and reaped in the same year a hundredfold." Read the Bible, and you'll walk away expecting good.

messages.text: Grace and peace are "multiplied to you in the knowledge of… Jesus our Lord," along with "all things that pertain to life and godliness."
messages.explanation:
Grace, unmerited favour, can increase, but Peter speaks of it being multiplied. Peace too, and its Hebrew counterpart shalom includes wholeness, health and well-being. How? Through epignosis, revelation knowledge of Jesus.

Notice the order: "all things that pertain to life and godliness." Much preaching covers godliness. But life comes first in this verse: provision, health, family, the practical things of everyday living. When you see Jesus in the Word by revelation, favour and peace multiply, and every part of your life benefits.

messages.text: His little girl was crying with a fever. He opened his Bible to pray for her, and got lost in how much the Father loves the Son.
messages.explanation:
When Jessica was about two, she had a viral infection and was crying in the next room. Joseph Prince went to pray, opened his Bible at random, and landed on Genesis 22: "Take now your son, your only son… whom you love." Reading it, he saw how much the Father loves Jesus, and that He didn't withhold Him from us. He began to weep, caught up in that love story, and forgot to keep praying about his daughter.

When he came to, she had stopped crying and fallen asleep, and the next day she was well. What he'd been anxiously striving for came naturally once he was occupied with Christ. Seeing Jesus isn't impractical; it's where practical answers flow from.

messages.text: The ram was caught in the thicket by its horns, not its fleece, so it stayed unblemished. A grown ram doesn't stumble in by accident.
messages.explanation:
An animal offered to God had to be without blemish. Had the ram been tangled by its wool, the thorns would have torn its skin. It was caught by its horns, and it was a mature ram, not a careless young lamb. Young animals blunder into trouble; a full-grown ram doesn't plunge into a thicket unless it means to.

Jesus said, "No one takes My life from Me, but I lay it down of Myself." On the same mountain range where Abraham offered the ram in Isaac's place, Jesus gave Himself willingly, spotless, in yours. "Abraham rejoiced to see My day," Jesus said; perhaps that's when he saw it.

messages.text: David took Goliath's head to Jerusalem. A thousand years later, Jesus was crucified at "the place of a skull."
messages.explanation:
The battle was in the Valley of Elah, miles from Jerusalem, a city then held by the Jebusites. Yet Scripture records that "David took the head of the Philistine and brought it to Jerusalem." Why carry it so far? Many have wondered whether it lies behind the name Golgotha.

The very first prophecy in the Bible said the woman's Seed would crush the serpent's head. At Calvary, Jesus, the greater Son of David, bore our sins and crushed the head of a far greater Goliath. The dragon-slayer has triumphed, and like David's men, you can stand unafraid behind your Captain.

messages.text: "The dead that he killed at his death were more than he had killed in his life." Jesus saved more by His death than in His whole ministry.
messages.explanation:
Samson often seems a poor picture of Christ. He was petty, impulsive and he tied foxes' tails together to burn the Philistines' fields. Sometimes you see Jesus by contrast: He sent His disciples out two by two to bring in the harvest, not destroy it.

But at the end, blinded and mocked, Samson stretched out his arms between two pillars and brought the temple down. Reading this to his little daughter, Joseph Prince suddenly saw it: Jesus stretched out His arms on the cross, and by His death brought far more salvation than in all His years of healing and teaching. "Unless a grain of wheat falls into the ground and dies, it remains alone."

messages.text: "Eat this scroll… and it was in my mouth like honey in sweetness." Read until the Word turns sweet.
messages.explanation:
God didn't tell Ezekiel to analyse the scroll but to eat it, and it tasted like honey. The first time Scripture speaks of something being made sweet is at Marah, where God turned bitter water sweet and said, "I am the Lord who heals you." Sweetness and healing go together: "Pleasant words are like a honeycomb, sweetness to the soul and health to the bones."

When you read, even a passage about judgment, keep going until you see God's heart and taste the sweetness. The Emmaus disciples called it a burning heart. "I sat down in His shade with great delight, and His fruit was sweet to my taste."

messages.text: The world looks ahead and sees death waiting. For you, death and judgment are behind you.
messages.explanation:
"He who hears My word and believes in Him who sent Me has everlasting life, and shall not come into judgment, but has passed from death into life." Most people try not to think about the end, but deep down they see it ahead of them. Your position is different: you died with Christ, and judgment fell on Him.

If Jesus tarries and this heart stops beating, you'll simply step into His presence, more alive than ever. And when He comes, the dead in Christ will rise and we'll receive bodies like His: forever young, forever strong. So your best years are always ahead. Enjoy every day as the high adventure it is.

messages.text: Paul lists the perilous last days, then gives the answer: "Continue in the things which you have learned… the Holy Scriptures."
messages.explanation:
"In the last days perilous times will come: for men will be lovers of themselves, lovers of money, boasters, proud." Wars start that way: my land, my pride. Scroll through social media and you'll see the boasting. The answer isn't panic or busyness, but the Word: Scriptures "able to make you wise for salvation," a word that includes healing, deliverance and wholeness.

The Scriptures make "the man of God complete, thoroughly equipped." The word for complete suggests being fitted out with a special aptitude, like a ship stocked for a long voyage. Spend time in the Word, and you'll find abilities and insights you never had before.

messages.text: "Move, or we'll run you down." "Sir, we can't. We're the lighthouse." You don't break God's Word; you break yourself against it.
messages.explanation:
In the old story, a naval commander sees a light ahead in the dark and orders it to change course. The reply comes back: "You change course." He announces his rank, his ship and its might. The answer: "We're a lighthouse." However impressive the vessel, the lighthouse isn't moving.

People call the Bible outdated, then science catches up with it. Doctors once bled the sick, believing it drew out disease; George Washington's death followed heavy bloodletting. Leviticus had long said, "The life of the flesh is in the blood." When a popular idea contradicts the Word, it's the idea that must bow.

messages.text: "If we sin wilfully after we have received the knowledge of the truth." Read the chapter around it: it's about turning away from Christ's sacrifice.
messages.explanation:
Many believers have been terrified by this verse. But be honest: isn't every sin you commit in some sense wilful? Miles Coverdale, who produced the first complete English Bible, advised readers to consider who is speaking, to whom, and "what goeth before and what followeth after."

Hebrews 10 says Christ "offered one sacrifice for sins forever" and that "there is no longer an offering for sin." It was written to Hebrews tempted to turn back from Jesus to the temple sacrifices. To know the truth and reject Christ's one sacrifice leaves no other sacrifice to turn to. That isn't you. For you, "their sins and their lawless deeds I will remember no more."

messages.text: The Shunammite gave Elisha a bed, a table, a stool and a lampstand. God's tabernacle had a table and a lampstand, but nowhere to sit.
messages.explanation:
The Shunammite woman furnished a little upper room for the prophet with four things. Two of them, the bed and the chair, are for rest. The tabernacle and the temple had a table and a lampstand, but no chair. The priests' work was never finished: "Every priest stands ministering daily and offering repeatedly the same sacrifices."

"But this Man, after He had offered one sacrifice for sins forever, sat down at the right hand of God." When you fail, Jesus doesn't stand up to die again; that would mean His sacrifice wasn't enough. Agree with Him: "One sacrifice for sins forever." That's true repentance, and then you move on.

messages.text: "You shall… clear out the old because of the new." Read the Old Testament through the New.
messages.explanation:
God promised Israel such abundant harvests that they'd still be eating last year's grain when the new crop came in, and would have to clear out the old to make room. It's also a principle for reading Scripture: bring the treasures of the Old Testament out in the light of the New.

When you read of judgment falling on someone, remember you're not under that covenant. When you read the sacrifices, see Christ crucified. When you read laws, ask what they reveal of Him and of God's heart. Without that, the Old Testament becomes a book of fear. With it, it's a treasure house of Jesus.

messages.text: Monday is coming. Go to work determined to make your company succeed, as working for the Lord.
messages.explanation:
Some believers think, "My boss isn't a Christian, so I'll do the minimum." Joseph served Potiphar and Pharaoh, neither of whom knew God, and made them prosper. They could see the Lord was with him. Think through problems, pray through them, find solutions; go the extra mile.

Not "with eyeservice, as men-pleasers," but "as to the Lord… knowing that from the Lord you will receive the reward of the inheritance." Believers have given the world flight, through the Wright brothers, sons of a preacher, and helped map the human genome. You have access to the God who gave Solomon wisdom, and favour no office politics can push down.

messages.text: Read the meanings of the names from Adam to Noah: "Man is appointed mortal sorrow, but the blessed God shall come down, teaching. His death shall bring the despairing rest."
messages.explanation:
Genesis 5 looks like a dull list of who lived how long. But take the names in order and look up their commonly given meanings: Adam, man; Seth, appointed; Enosh, mortal; Kenan, sorrow; Mahalalel, the blessed God; Jared, shall come down; Enoch, teaching; Methuselah, his death shall bring; Lamech, often linked with despair or power; Noah, rest.

Read together, they tell the gospel in the very first pages of Scripture, long before the cross. God hides treasure even in names. Ask Him to open your eyes, and dull chapters can light up with Jesus.

messages.text: Methuselah's name has been read as "when he dies, it will come." He lived 969 years, longer than anyone in Scripture.
messages.explanation:
Enoch walked with God after his son Methuselah was born, as if the name itself were a prophecy, pointing to the judgment of the flood. Imagine the household holding its breath every time the boy fell sick. And yet God let him live longer than any other man on record.

The flood came in the year Methuselah died. God must execute justice, or evil runs unchecked. But His heart is love, and He waited and waited. "The Lord is not slack concerning His promise… but is longsuffering toward us, not willing that any should perish." He's still that patient today.

messages.text: The word in prayer was "creative miracles": what's worn out, removed or missing, God can make new.
messages.explanation:
Praying the night before the service, Joseph Prince kept hearing two words: creative miracles. Not just healing of what's sick, but recreation of what's gone: an organ that's been removed, a spine that's degenerated, a mind that's growing foggy. Doctors do their best with natural means, and we thank God for them.

But Jesus said, "With men it is impossible, but not with God; for with God all things are possible." If you've received a hard report, don't accept it as the final word. Ask Him for a creative miracle, then step out and do what you couldn't do before.

messages.text: "Do not be afraid; only believe." Before Jesus healed, He often dealt with fear first.
messages.explanation:
Messengers came to Jairus with the worst news a father could hear: "Your daughter is dead. Why trouble the Teacher any further?" Jesus overheard and immediately said, "Do not be afraid; only believe." Then He went in and raised her.

If you've just had a bad report from the doctor, hear Him say the same to you. Fear shrinks your expectation; faith opens the door. People of the world look ahead as they age and see only decline. You have a different future. He wants you well now, and eternal life awaits you.

messages.text: Revelation foretold an event in Jerusalem that the whole world would watch. For centuries that seemed impossible.
messages.explanation:
When John wrote it, Jerusalem was about to be destroyed, and for nearly two thousand years it lay largely desolate; Mark Twain described the land as barren and forsaken. Scripture said the people of every nation would see something happen there. Who could imagine the world watching one street in one city? And who would rebuild Jerusalem?

The Jews returned and Israel was reborn in 1948, and today live broadcasts reach every nation in an instant. Scripture describes wars and rumours of wars, plagues and great earthquakes increasing in the last days. Don't be afraid like those without hope. The Word you hold is more advanced than any headline.

messages.text: Being male is a matter of birth. Being a man is a matter of choice.
messages.explanation:
In a culture that blurs God's design, go back to the original: "Male and female He created them." God wasn't confused. To the men: don't let anyone shame you out of your masculinity. Take responsibility. Protect your wife and children. If you're afraid, do it afraid. And if your wife needs to win the argument, let her; that's part of being a man too.

Teach your sons, as they grow, to honour and care for women. And a woman's femininity flourishes most when her man is allowed to be a man. "Watch, stand fast in the faith, be brave, be strong."

messages.text: Bees kept getting into his toddler's room. He drew a line in Jesus' name, and the next morning dead bees lay along it.
messages.explanation:
In a rented home, bees came in through the balcony at night, and his little daughter would wake up hearing them buzz. Joseph Prince walked the room, anointed the windows with oil, and declared a bloodline of Jesus across her bed area. The next day the family found dead bees along the line. They hadn't crossed.

"When I see the blood, I will pass over you." The blood of Jesus isn't a vague religious idea; it's what covers you and your family. Every time he boards a plane, he quietly lays his hand on it and covers it with the blood. Don't take your safety for granted. Plead the blood over what God has given you.

messages.text: The giants were still in the land and the Jordan was in flood. God told Joshua to be occupied with His Word, not the enemy.
messages.explanation:
Moses had just died. The same enemies that frightened Israel forty years earlier were still there, more entrenched than ever. Jericho's walls were thick, and the Jordan overflowed its banks at harvest time: the worst possible moment to cross. Yet God's first instruction to Joshua said nothing about strategy: "This Book of the Law shall not depart from your mouth, but you shall meditate in it day and night… then you will make your way prosperous, and then you will have good success."

Whatever obstacle is in front of you, don't be engrossed with it. Be occupied with His Word. And good success never steals your family, your church or your peace. It's money working for you, not you slaving for money.

messages.text: An elderly woman walked home from church singing hymns. The witches in the field saw a ball of light pass by.
messages.explanation:
It's said that in a place where witchcraft was still practised, a group was in the middle of an open-air ritual, drums beating, when their leader suddenly fell on her face, trembling and whimpering. Behind them, an old lady was walking home along a path, quietly singing. The others saw only her; the leader said she'd seen a ball of light pass by.

You don't know your own influence. People who don't yet know Jesus are often drawn to be near a believer without knowing why. There's stability there, and they feel lifted after time with you. You're a light, going somewhere to shine.

messages.text: He jumped the fence to run across the greenest field he'd ever seen. Up close, it was full of sheep droppings.
messages.explanation:
Travelling in New Zealand, Joseph Prince asked his friends to stop the car so he could run across a hillside so green it looked unreal. Halfway across he stopped and looked down at his shoes. From the road, you couldn't see what was in the grass.

Someone else's marriage, job or country always looks greener, and social media is designed to make you feel your life is the only grey one. People in New York weep over a plate of Singapore food; Singaporeans dream of New York. "Godliness with contentment is great gain." Your life is too precious to spend comparing it with a filtered picture.

messages.text: "Strengthened with all might, according to His glorious power"—for what? "For all patience and longsuffering with joy."
messages.explanation:
Look at the words Paul piles up: might, power, glory. We'd expect it to be for miracles. Instead, it's "for all patience" (endurance under hard circumstances) "and longsuffering" (makrothumia, literally a long temper, patience with people) "with joy."

That's how much it matters to God how you treat people. Letting a bus pull out in front of you, forgiving the drivers who honk, being kind when someone doesn't deserve it: these please Him more than visible service done to be seen. Pray this for yourself and those you love. If at first you manage patience without the joy, keep going; it's growing.

messages.text: "Study to show yourself approved." In ancient Greece, "approved" described money changers who refused clipped coins.
messages.explanation:
Coins were made of soft metal, and dishonest people shaved bits off the edges; Athens passed many laws trying to stop it. Honest money changers refused to accept clipped coins. They were called dokimos, tested and approved, people of integrity.

That's the word Paul uses for those who teach God's Word: "a worker who does not need to be ashamed, rightly dividing the word of truth." It isn't about earning God's acceptance; you're already accepted in Christ. It's about handling Scripture with integrity, without shaving bits off or adding to it, so that what you pass on is genuine.

messages.text: Jesus said Sodom would have repented if it had seen His miracles. The key to reaching people far from God is the power of God.
messages.explanation:
Capernaum saw the blind see and the dead raised, yet rejected Him, and Jesus said that if those miracles had been done in Sodom, "it would have remained until this day." Rejecting grace is worse than Sodom's sin. But hidden in that rebuke is a key: miracles move hearts that arguments can't reach.

Don't judge people trapped in destructive lifestyles. Pray for them, and release God's power. "They will lay hands on the sick, and they will recover." Your part is the hands and the laying on. Their part is to recover, whether that day or in the days that follow. The healing power is His.

messages.text: "God sent forth His Son… born under the law." Read Jesus' earthly words in the light of who He was speaking to.
messages.explanation:
Before the cross, Jesus sent the twelve out with instructions: "Do not go into the way of the Gentiles… but go rather to the lost sheep of the house of Israel." Those words are printed in red in many Bibles, yet no one applies them today, because after His resurrection He said, "Go therefore and make disciples of all the nations."

Jesus was born under the law to redeem those under the law. His earthly ministry fulfilled God's promises to Israel first. The Gospels are precious for seeing Him clearly. But the letters to the churches are equally the words of the ascended Christ, given through His apostles. Rightly divide the Word, and much confusion clears.

messages.text: If his grandfather hadn't pulled his three-year-old mother out of the sea, he wouldn't exist. Your life is bound up with your head, Adam or Christ.
messages.explanation:
Joseph Prince's mother fell into choppy water as a toddler, and her father, dressed for a party, ran and dived in after her. If she'd drowned, her son would never have been born. Like it or not, what your forefathers did shapes you. That's why Adam's fall affects every one of us: he was the head of the human race.

So God sent a second Adam. The first, surrounded by paradise, gave everything away for a piece of fruit; Jesus, alone in the wilderness, overcame. Stop identifying with the old head: "My father had this condition, so I'll have it too." If you're born again, Christ is your head now. "As He is, so are we in this world."

messages.text: A few days after carrying the world's sins, Jesus walked into heaven and sat down. Where are those sins now?
messages.explanation:
No one in history bore more sin than Jesus did on the cross: every filth and every failure, including yours. Then, risen, He entered the Father's presence with His own blood, "having obtained eternal redemption," and the Father said, "Sit at My right hand."

"When He had by Himself purged our sins, sat down at the right hand of the Majesty on high." He couldn't sit there if the sins were still on Him. The fact that Jesus is seated is your proof that they're gone. God's eye is on that blood, and as long as it's there, He doesn't count your sins against you.

messages.text: You're never an absentee worshipper. In Christ, you're always in the Holy of Holies.
messages.explanation:
Aaron could enter the Most Holy Place once a year, trembling, knowing that a careless sin meant death. You're seated with Christ in the heavenly places, permanently. It's "a new and living way": the more you come, the more you live.

Jewellers display gems under bright lights because the light brings out their brilliance. In God's presence, His light doesn't expose you to condemn you; "the blood of Jesus Christ His Son cleanses us from all sin" while we walk in that light. It shows how perfectly Jesus has made you clean. So when you pray, don't start as if you've been far away. You're already there.

messages.text: The deepest way to deal with a bad habit isn't in fear outside God's presence. It's as a son, inside it.
messages.explanation:
Under the law, you dealt with sin trembling, unsure if you were acceptable. Under grace, you're already accepted forever, so you can be honest: "Father, I've got a bad temper. That wasn't good. Work on me here." That's not excusing sin; it's judging it in the light of His love.

Overcoming the habit isn't the condition for His acceptance. It's a testimony to the world that you're becoming more like Jesus. A child who knows he's loved can bring his worst moments to his father without hiding. "You did not receive the spirit of bondage again to fear, but… the Spirit of adoption."

messages.text: You can't stop birds flying over your head. You can stop them building a nest there.
messages.explanation:
Even in your holiest moments, praying or taking communion, a shocking thought can flash through your mind. Sometimes it's the flesh, sometimes the enemy. The devil says, "See? That's the real you." It isn't. "You are not in the flesh but in the Spirit."

Don't be horrified into treating it as alive. Like stepping off a boat after a day at sea, you may still feel the sway for a while, but you're on solid ground. Say, "That's not me. My old man was crucified with Christ." Reckon it dead, refuse to entertain it, and keep your eyes on Jesus.

messages.text: Praying "in Jesus' name" isn't a magic phrase at the end. It's praying from His position.
messages.explanation:
Look at Paul's prayers recorded in his letters: many don't end with the words "in Jesus' name." That isn't wrong to say; please keep saying it. But Jesus meant more than a formula. To pray in His name is to pray as His representative, standing where He stands, as accepted as He is.

If you pray as though God is far away and you're struggling to reach Him, you're praying from a false premise, and the Spirit of truth can't bear witness with it. Begin from the truth: "Father," spoken as someone near. You're seated with Christ. Pray from there.

messages.text: Faith isn't pretending something exists. It's acting as if what God says is true, because it already is.
messages.explanation:
Your feelings fluctuate: some days prayer feels powerful, some days flat. Some days you're sure you're close to God, others you feel far away. Feelings aren't reality. "The things which are seen are temporary, but the things which are not seen are eternal."

You can't conjure something out of nothing by believing hard enough; only God creates from nothing. Faith walks in line with what He's already established in the unseen. Act as if you're forgiven, because you are. Act as if you're righteous, because the gift of righteousness is yours. Act as if your prayers matter, because they do.

messages.text: Across her medical report she wrote: "Does Jesus have lumps in His breast? As He is, so am I." At her next checkup, it was gone.
messages.explanation:
A woman in the church was told she had a breast tumour suspected to be cancerous. She brought the report to Joseph Prince with those words written on it. When she went back for her next examination, the lump had disappeared. Her testimony went on to encourage many other women who heard it.

The verse doesn't say "as He was," walking by Galilee, but "as He is": risen, glorified, seated at the Father's right hand, free from every sickness and every sin He once bore. Whatever you're facing, ask: does Jesus have this now? Then say what God says: "As He is, so am I in this world."

messages.text: "Your adversary the devil walks about like a roaring lion." Lions don't attack the herd. They wait for a straggler.
messages.explanation:
Watch a lion on the savannah: it moves slowly and patiently. It doesn't charge a strong, united herd. It watches for one that's injured, confused or lagging behind, and waits until that one is isolated.

There's a protection in being together with God's people that's hard to explain but very real. Someone says a word that breaks the depression you've carried all week; you're lifted just by being among believers. "Not forsaking the assembling of ourselves together… and so much the more as you see the Day approaching." Where brothers dwell together in unity, "there the Lord commanded the blessing."

messages.text: God saw darkness and didn't describe it. He said, "Let there be light." Faith calls things that are not as though they were.
messages.explanation:
God changed Abram's name to Abraham, "father of many nations," before Sarah had even conceived. Imagine her calling him in from the fields: "Father of many, dinner's ready!" The neighbours must have pitied them. But Abraham believed God, "who gives life to the dead and calls those things which do not exist as though they did."

People mock this as "name it and claim it." Yes, there are silly extremes. But Jesus didn't announce what He saw; He called forth what He wanted to see: "Stretch out your hand." Everything visible came from the invisible. Speak God's Word over your situation before you see it.

messages.text: The Hebrew word for bless, barak, has been defined as "to endue with beneficial power" for success, prosperity, fruitfulness and long life.
messages.explanation:
When God told Isaac, "I will be with you and bless you," what did that mean? Hebrew scholars describe barak as God conferring beneficial power that brings fruitfulness to people, livestock and land, security from enemies, and well-being. It's closely tied to shalom, which one lexicon says can be translated prosperity, well-being, health, completeness and safety.

The blessing begins with being made right with God; that's the greatest prosperity. But it doesn't stop at the spiritual. It touches your body, your family and your work, so that you can be a blessing: "I will bless you… and you shall be a blessing."

messages.text: "How hard it is for those who trust in riches to enter the kingdom of God." You can love money without having any.
messages.explanation:
The disciples, who had a fishing business with partners, were astonished when Jesus said it was hard for the rich to enter the kingdom. So He clarified: "Children, how hard it is for those who trust in riches." Scripture doesn't say money is the root of all evil, but "the love of money." And many with empty pockets think about money constantly; money has become the voice they obey.

One way to break money's hold on your heart is to honour God with the first part of what you receive. It's a declaration that however blessed you are, He is your source. Let money serve you; never let it master you.

messages.text: "Though He was rich, yet for your sakes He became poor, that you through His poverty might become rich." Read the chapters around it: it's about giving.
messages.explanation:
Taken alone, the verse could be read as purely spiritual. But Paul places it right in the middle of a collection for poor believers in Jerusalem. He praises the Macedonians who gave beyond their ability, calls giving "this grace also," and goes on: "He who sows bountifully will also reap bountifully… God loves a cheerful giver."

The One who flung the galaxies into space died with nothing, and soldiers gambled for His clothes. He bore your sins, your sicknesses and your poverty, that you might receive His righteousness, health and riches. Not to hoard them like the Dead Sea, but to be a channel always looking for a chance to give.

messages.text: "The blessing of the Lord makes one rich, and He adds no sorrow with it."
messages.explanation:
The word for sorrow can mean painful toil. Some "success" costs your sleep, your health and your peace: eyes glued to the charts, stomach knotted with stress. God's blessing isn't like that. There's still work and effort, like healthy exercise that leaves you pleasantly tired, but not the crushing kind that breaks you.

When famine came, God's first word to Isaac was, "Do not go down to Egypt": don't run to the world's ways. Beware of anything that promises quick riches but robs your rest. If you're constantly stressed and in strife over it, it isn't God. His way leads to a full cup and a quiet heart.

messages.text: In a great famine, Elijah was sent to a widow from Jezebel's homeland. Of all Israel's lepers, only Naaman the Syrian was healed. Nazareth was furious.
messages.explanation:
In His hometown synagogue, Jesus read, "He has anointed Me to preach the gospel to the poor… to heal the brokenhearted." No one objected. Then He gave two examples: Elijah was sent not to Israel's widows but to one in the region of Sidon, the homeland of Jezebel, and Elisha cleansed not Israel's lepers but the commander of an enemy army. They tried to throw Him off a cliff.

Those two examples still provoke religious people: grace given to the undeserving, and blessing that's tangible, provision for a starving widow and healing for a leper. But that's the gospel. What's good news to the poor if not that supply is coming?

messages.text: "The Lord is my shepherd; I shall not want." The Hebrew for lack and the Hebrew for grace differ by one letter: one ends with a head, the other with a door.
messages.explanation:
The word for "want" or lack is chaser. Its last letter, resh, pictures a head. Life supported by your own head, your own reasoning and calculations, ends in lack. Change that final letter to dalet, which pictures a door, and you get chesed: grace, lovingkindness.

Jesus said, "I am the door. If anyone enters by Me, he will be saved, and will go in and out and find pasture." God gave you a mind, and He wants you to use it. But let your spirit be led by Him first, and let your mind follow. Life that flows through the Door doesn't run dry.

messages.text: The devil doesn't say "You can't provide for your family." He whispers "I can't," so you'll think it's your own thought.
messages.explanation:
Thoughts of fear and condemnation come at you in the first person: "I'm an addict. I'll never sleep well. I can't provide for my family in this recession." Because they sound like your own voice, you own them, and they weigh you down.

Jesus said, "Do not worry, saying, 'What shall we eat?'" The thought will come, but you take it by saying it. So refuse to agree with it out loud. A believer can't be possessed, but can be harassed from outside. Recognise those thoughts for what they are, and answer them with what God says about you.

messages.text: On their last night in Egypt, God gave Israel favour, and the Egyptians handed them silver and gold: four hundred years of back pay in one night.
messages.explanation:
Israel had laboured for generations without wages. Then, on the night of the final plague, "the Lord had given the people favour in the sight of the Egyptians," and they left with silver, gold and clothing. What was it for? To build God's tabernacle. While Moses was on the mountain receiving the pattern, the enemy distracted them into making a golden calf. Yet even after that, they had so much left that Moses had to tell them to stop giving.

We may be the generation living on the last night before we leave. God isn't against His people having wealth; He's looking for those He can trust to use it for His purposes: for the gospel, His house and the poor.

messages.text: In Hebrew idiom, an "evil eye" means stinginess, and a "good eye" means generosity. Jesus said a good eye fills your whole body with light.
messages.explanation:
"A man with an evil eye hastens after riches, and does not consider that poverty will come upon him." "He who has a generous eye will be blessed, for he gives of his bread to the poor." When the vineyard workers grumbled at the owner's generosity, he asked, "Is your eye evil because I am good?"

So when Jesus said, "When your eye is good, your whole body also is full of light," the word for body is the physical body. Then He told a Pharisee obsessed with outward washing, "Give alms of such things as you have; then indeed all things are clean to you." Generosity touches you inside and out.

messages.text: "Dip seven times in the Jordan?" Naaman was offended. When he humbled himself, his flesh became like a little child's.
messages.explanation:
The great Syrian commander expected Elisha to come out and wave his hand over him. Instead, a messenger told him to wash seven times in the muddy little Jordan. "Are not the rivers of Damascus better?" A wise servant said, "If the prophet had told you to do something great, would you not have done it?"

He swallowed his pride and dipped once, twice, six times, with nothing to show for it. On the seventh, "his flesh was restored like the flesh of a little child." God's ways often bypass our logic. "By humility and the fear of the Lord are riches and honour and life." Keep dipping.

messages.text: Would you want your children greedy? No. Would you want them sick and always struggling? Of course not. Neither does your Father.
messages.explanation:
Some people mock the "health and wealth gospel," and there are extremes worth rejecting: preaching that's all about money for self. But ask any parent what they want for their child. You'd want them healthy, with more than enough, and generous rather than selfish. When their own children fall ill, even critics of healing rush them to the doctor.

Jesus appealed to that very instinct: "If you then, being evil, know how to give good gifts to your children, how much more will your Father who is in heaven give good things to those who ask Him!" Don't let fear of excess rob a whole generation of trusting God to provide and heal.

messages.text: "Where your treasure is, there your heart will be also." Your heart follows your money, not the other way around.
messages.explanation:
We often say people put their money where their heart is. Jesus put it the other way: put your treasure somewhere, and your heart will follow it there. If your heart isn't yet stirred about the gospel, start sowing into it anyway, by faith, and watch your heart move.

In a famine, gospel ground can look like cracked, dry earth, a poor investment compared with whatever seems green and promising. Isaac sowed in a land of famine, "and reaped in the same year a hundredfold." Faith sows where sight says nothing will grow.

messages.text: "The wealth of the sinner is stored up for the righteous." To the sinner God gives "the work of gathering and collecting."
messages.explanation:
"God gives wisdom and knowledge and joy to a man who is good in His sight; but to the sinner He gives the work of gathering and collecting, that he may give to him who is good before God." Don't envy the wicked as they pile it up. In God's economy, it's being stored for someone else.

God always does it justly, never by cheating or manipulation. Often the transfer happens the best way of all: the sinner gets saved, and their resources come into God's kingdom with them. Who are the righteous? Everyone made righteous by the blood of Jesus, and that includes you.

messages.text: Four centuries ahead, God told Abraham his descendants would be slaves, then added, "Afterward they shall come out with great possessions."
messages.explanation:
When God appears in a dream, His words are few and chosen. Of all He could have told Abraham about the future, He included this: they would leave with great possessions. And it happened, not at the start or middle of the plagues, but on the night of the last one: "The Lord had given the people favour in the sight of the Egyptians."

That wealth had a purpose from the beginning: it built God's tabernacle. Prosperity in Scripture is never just to be hoarded. It's back pay with interest, entrusted to people who'll use it for His house.

messages.text: "It is He who gives you power to get wealth, that He may establish His covenant which He swore to your fathers": the covenant of grace.
messages.explanation:
God warned Israel not to say "in your heart," "My power and the might of my hand have gained me this wealth." Why would anyone think that? Because the power God gives often looks completely natural: a wise investment, a promotion, a client who simply prefers you. It's supernaturally natural, so it's easy to forget its source.

And its purpose: "to establish His covenant which He swore to your fathers." Not the law of Sinai, which came 430 years later, but the unconditional promise to Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, the covenant of grace that we live under now. Wherever that grace is being proclaimed, that's where the power to get wealth is meant to flow.

messages.text: "Sinners shall not stand in the congregation of the righteous." Perhaps because by then, they'll have become righteous.
messages.explanation:
Joseph Prince used to read Psalm 1 as a picture of the ungodly swept away. Then it struck him: sinners won't stand in the congregation of the righteous because they'll have been made righteous. That's the gospel's goal: the lost brought in.

But "how shall they hear without a preacher? And how shall they preach unless they are sent?" This is where the gospel and money meet. Broadcasts, buildings, plane tickets, Bibles: none of it happens without resources. When you give to spread the gospel, you're helping fill that congregation.

messages.text: While Moses was on the mountain receiving the pattern for God's house, the people below melted their gold into a calf.
messages.explanation:
"As for this Moses… we do not know what has become of him." Moses was gone longer than they expected, and their gold, given for God's dwelling, was poured into an idol. The devil didn't take their wealth away; he redirected it.

Jesus warned of a servant who says in his heart, "My master is delaying his coming," and starts behaving badly. When the hope of Christ's return grows dim, God's people drift. Your resources will go somewhere this month. The enemy would love to divert them into some golden calf. Keep your eyes on Jesus, who is coming back, and on what He's building.

messages.text: "Good measure, pressed down, shaken together, and running over." Jesus described the return in detail because He wants you to expect it.
messages.explanation:
Some say it's wrong to give expecting to receive. But why would Jesus describe the harvest so vividly if He didn't want you encouraged by it? Why would Genesis record that Isaac "began to prosper, and continued prospering until he became very prosperous"? No one tells a farmer it's selfish to expect a crop from his seed.

The running over is the point. Good measure fills the container; running over spills out to others. God gives more than enough so you can be a channel, like the Sea of Galilee teeming with life, not the Dead Sea that only receives.

messages.text: "If God is for us, who can be against us?" The Greek word can also mean "what." What can be against you?
messages.explanation:
The Greek word tis, translated "who" here, is used far more often in the New Testament as "what." So you can read it both ways: who can be against me, and what can be against me? A recession? A disease? Your guilt? Satan himself? Whatever the coming year brings, none of it can succeed against you if God is for you.

God for us: never did three little words mean so much. Not watching from a distance, not waiting to pounce, but on your side. If that's true, you can rest. You're loved, and you're taken care of.

messages.text: God didn't wait for you to behave before He gave you His Son.
messages.explanation:
Maybe you think, "God is for Christians, but not for me. I've ignored Him, rebelled against Him, even blasphemed His name." Yet God gave His Son while the world was going its own merry way. His love isn't switched off by your sin; your sin is the very reason He sent Jesus.

"For God so loved the world." Unless you can prove you're not part of the world, that verse has your name in it. Put it there and read it again. The first proof that God is for you is the gift of His Son.

messages.text: Adam and Eve covered themselves with fig leaves. God covered them with skins. The first sacrifice was made by God Himself.
messages.explanation:
When man sinned, the glory of God that clothed him departed, and Adam and Eve felt naked and exposed. Their fix was leaves: a bloodless covering of their own making. But "without shedding of blood there is no remission." So God Himself slew an animal and clothed them with its skin.

What man provides is never complete. What God provides is perfect and lasting, because He is. That first innocent substitute pointed to the true Lamb of God, who takes away the sin of the world. You don't have to stitch together a covering of good works. God has already provided one.

messages.text: The guilty man laid his hands on the innocent lamb. His sins went to the lamb; the lamb's acceptance came to him.
messages.explanation:
Under the old covenant, the sinner placed his hands on the lamb's head. That act identified the lamb with his guilt. The lamb hadn't done anything wrong, yet it became chargeable, and when the fire fell on the altar, the worshipper was accepted. The lamb didn't deserve to die. The sinner didn't deserve to go free. That's grace.

When you believe on Jesus, it's like laying your hands on the true Lamb. "He made Him who knew no sin to be sin for us, that we might become the righteousness of God in Him." All you deserved fell on Him. All He deserves now comes to you.

messages.text: God didn't raise Jesus because He was God's Son, or because He lived a perfect life. He raised Him because you were declared righteous.
messages.explanation:
"He was delivered up because of our offences, and was raised because of our justification." Young's Literal Translation puts it, "raised up because of our being declared righteous." Days earlier, Jesus had been chargeable with every sin you've ever committed. If even one remained on Him, God couldn't have raised Him.

So the empty tomb is God's receipt. Your sins were removed so completely that the One who carried them could walk out alive. Let that settle your heart: the resurrection is proof that you've been declared righteous, apart from your works.

messages.text: At Sinai, the law came in one language. At Pentecost, the good news came in every listener's mother tongue.
messages.explanation:
The crowd in Jerusalem was amazed: "How is it that we hear, each in our own language in which we were born?" The Greek word is dialektos, the dialect you heard as a baby when your mother whispered love to you. The Holy Spirit chose the most intimate language each person had.

The law, given in one tongue, was all about what man must do: "You shall not… you shall not." At Pentecost they heard "the wonderful works of God." Grace isn't about your puny works but about His. And God wants it to reach you so personally that you can't miss His love.

messages.text: "God helps those who help themselves" isn't in the Bible. God helps the helpless.
messages.explanation:
Our problem is that we don't think we're helpless enough. So we go round the same mountain, bump into the same wall, and keep going back to things we know won't satisfy. Grace is unearned, undeserved favour, and it starts where your own strength ends.

A man in the church was bound to alcohol, often too drunk to know how he got home. One day, resting after a game of squash, the sweet presence of the Lord came over him, and the desire to drink was simply taken away. No course of discipline, no striving. That's grace, and the whole Christian life is meant to be lived that way.

messages.text: The eyes of the Lord your God are on you from the beginning of the year to the very end of it, not to find fault, but to bless.
messages.explanation:
Moses described the promised land as "a land for which the Lord your God cares; the eyes of the Lord your God are always on it, from the beginning of the year to the very end of the year." If God cared like that for a piece of land, how much more for you, His child?

You don't know what the year holds, but you know who holds it. His eyes aren't searching you for faults. He'll guide you where you're going wrong, yes, but His gaze is there to favour you, lead you, protect you and provide for you, every day from January to December.

messages.text: Forgetfulness isn't simply "getting old." It came with the fall, and Christ redeemed your mind too. Say, "I have the mind of Christ."
messages.explanation:
Adam named every animal God brought to him and remembered them all. Jesus, without owning a scroll, had absorbed the Scriptures so well that He answered the devil instantly: "It is written." The decline of the mind, like sickness and death, came in through the fall. We laugh about "senior moments," but don't accept them as normal.

You're a spirit, you have a soul, and you live in a body, and Jesus redeemed all three. When a name won't come, don't say, "I'm getting old." Say, "I have the mind of Christ." It may not come instantly, but keep releasing faith. Like seed, it comes thirtyfold, sixtyfold, a hundredfold.

messages.text: Before the thief can kill and destroy, he has to steal. What does he steal? The word you heard but didn't understand.
messages.explanation:
A burglar doesn't go for the toilet rolls; he goes for the diamonds. Jesus said, "When anyone hears the word of the kingdom, and does not understand it, then the wicked one comes and snatches away what was sown in his heart." Before the enemy can touch your body, he needs the word of healing out of your head.

The good ground is the one who "hears the word and understands it." The Greek word is suniēmi: to put things together, to see what God is showing you. A tiny seed can split concrete if it's given time to sprout. So keep hearing, and ask God for understanding until the word takes root.

messages.text: Don't let His words depart from your eyes; keep them in your heart. "They are life to those who find them, and health to all their flesh."
messages.explanation:
God's word enters through two gates: your ears and your eyes. Seeing it doesn't mean walking down the street with your nose in a Bible; it means picturing what it says. When it says you're a tree planted by rivers of water, see yourself that way. When it says you'll bear fruit in old age, see yourself green and full of sap.

Keep hearing and seeing it until it drops into your heart. Jesus said of those who close their eyes, "lest they should understand with their hearts and turn, so that I should heal them." When the word is understood in the heart, healing follows. And it's health to "all" your flesh, from your head to your knees.

messages.text: "Length of days is in her right hand, in her left hand riches and honour." Wisdom is worth more than any market.
messages.explanation:
Wisdom has nothing to do with IQ. Brilliant people still wreck their marriages and their health. Wisdom comes from God, and Scripture pictures her as a woman holding gifts in both hands: long life in the right, the hand of priority; riches and honour in the left; and "all her paths are peace."

Solomon asked only for an understanding heart, and God said, "I have also given you what you have not asked: both riches and honour." Wisdom isn't really an "it" but a Person: Christ is our wisdom. Ask Him for it. Seeking wisdom first brings everything else you were going to ask for.

messages.text: When Solomon woke from the dream in which he received wisdom, the first thing he did was go and stand before the ark.
messages.explanation:
Solomon was at Gibeon, where the tabernacle of Moses stood: all the outward structure of worship, but without the ark of the covenant. The ark, gold over wood with the blood-sprinkled mercy seat on top, pictures Jesus: fully God, fully man, and our atonement.

Once Solomon had wisdom, he left the place of religious trappings and went to Jerusalem to stand in the presence of the ark. That's the first sign of true wisdom: you're no longer content with the form of religion. You want the reality: Jesus Himself. Wise men still seek Him.

messages.text: You tell Him, "Your love is better than wine." He answers, "How much better than wine is your love!" He always exceeds you.
messages.explanation:
The bride says to the bridegroom, "Let him kiss me with the kisses of his mouth, for your love is better than wine": better than every earthly celebration and harvest. Then, a few chapters later, the bridegroom turns her words around: "How much better than wine is your love!"

Your love for Jesus is imperfect; His is perfect. Yet He treasures whatever little love you have. When mothers asked Jesus just to touch their children, "He took them up in His arms" and blessed them. Ask Him for a little, and He gives a lot. In everything, even in love, He outdoes you.

messages.text: "The race is not to the swift, nor the battle to the strong… but time and chance happen to them all." Only God can put you at the right place at the right time.
messages.explanation:
The wisest man who ever lived observed that the fastest don't always win, the skilled don't always get the favour, and the smartest don't always get rich. What makes the difference is being in the right place at the right time: meeting an old friend who just happens to need someone like you, or arriving just when a door opens.

No amount of cleverness can arrange that. Only God can, whether it's opening an opportunity or steering you away from a tragedy you never knew was ahead. That's why it's better to trust in the Lord than to put confidence in man. Ask Him to order your timing.

messages.text: Chronos is time on the clock. Kairos is the right time: the opportune, favourable moment. God has kairos moments for you.
messages.explanation:
The Greek Old Testament translates the "time" of Ecclesiastes 9:11 with kairos. Chronos measures time in numbers: one o'clock, ten years. Kairos describes time by its quality: a seasonable, opportune moment, the time when something is ripe.

Peter promised that when people turn to God, "times of refreshing may come from the presence of the Lord." Those times are kairos too. Not every day will feel like one, but as you stay in His presence, expect seasons of refreshing and moments that open up in a way only He could arrange.

messages.text: The Hebrew word for the right time first appears when the dove returned to Noah "in the evening," with a fresh olive leaf in her mouth.
messages.explanation:
By the law of first mention, the first time a word appears in Scripture often sets its meaning. The first use of et, the Hebrew for a right or opportune time, is when the dove comes back to the ark, and Noah knows the judgment is over and the waters have receded.

The dove is a picture of the Holy Spirit. He's the One who orchestrates events and circumstances to put you in the right place at the right time. So learn to listen for His inner green light and His peace before you sign, decide or commit, in small things as well as big ones. You're not stepping into the year alone.

messages.text: "In due season we shall reap if we do not lose heart." Due season is kairos. If you've waited long, don't faint now.
messages.explanation:
Abraham and Sarah waited over twenty years. Then the Lord said, "I will return to you according to the time of life, and Sarah shall have a son." When Paul quoted it in Romans, the word for that appointed time was kairos. "Is anything too hard for the Lord?" can be read, "Is anything too wonderful for Him?"

You may have been believing God for something for years with only small improvements. The timing of the harvest is His, but the promise is sure. Don't grow weary. And when your kairos comes, Paul adds, "as we have opportunity" (kairos again), "let us do good to all."

messages.text: Ruth said, "Let me glean after him in whose sight I shall find grace." Then "her hap was to light" on the field of Boaz.
messages.explanation:
Ruth was a Moabite widow in a strange town, with only the most back-breaking work open to her. By the law she was disqualified, but she set out expecting grace.
